content.stem: Magnetic particle testing detects discontinuities that are:
options: At or near the surface of ferromagnetic parts
Deep within the interior of any solid material
Only in nonmagnetic metals such as aluminum
Only in plastics and other nonmetal materials
content.explanation: MT reveals surface-breaking and slightly subsurface discontinuities in ferromagnetic materials. It does not find deep internal flaws and does not work on nonmagnetic materials.
distractors: MT is limited to surface and near-surface flaws, not deep internal ones.
MT requires a ferromagnetic (magnetic) material, not nonmagnetic metals.
Plastics are not ferromagnetic and cannot be inspected by MT.

content.stem: MT can only be used on materials that are:
options: Ferromagnetic materials such as steel
Nonmagnetic materials such as aluminum
Porous materials that soak up liquid
Transparent materials that pass light
content.explanation: Only ferromagnetic materials such as carbon steels and many irons can be magnetized enough to hold a leakage field at a flaw. The elements nickel and cobalt are also ferromagnetic, but many nickel alloys (for example austenitic grades such as Inconel) are nonmagnetic and need PT. Aluminum and austenitic stainless are not ferromagnetic.
distractors: Nonmagnetic materials cannot be magnetized for MT; PT is used instead.
Porosity is unrelated to whether MT can be applied; magnetism is the requirement.
Transparency has nothing to do with magnetic particle testing.

content.stem: MT detects a discontinuity because it causes:
options: A flux leakage field that draws particles to it
An electric spark that jumps across the flaw
A visible color change in the metal at the flaw
A faint audible sound emitted from the flaw
content.explanation: A discontinuity interrupts the magnetic flux, forcing some flux out at the surface. This leakage field attracts magnetic particles, forming an indication.
distractors: MT does not rely on electric sparks to detect flaws.
MT works by particle attraction to a leakage field, not a color change in the metal.
MT produces a visible particle buildup, not a sound.

content.stem: A flux leakage field forms at a discontinuity because the discontinuity:
options: Interrupts the flux and forces some out of the surface
Conducts electric current away from the flawed region
Heats the surrounding metal right at the flaw location
Adds extra magnetism into the body of the part itself
content.explanation: Where a flaw breaks the flux path, the flux is forced out and back into the part, creating north and south leakage poles that hold particles.
distractors: The effect is magnetic flux leakage, not electrical conduction.
Leakage is a magnetic effect, not heating.
The flaw distorts existing flux; it does not add magnetism.

content.stem: Magnetic particles form an indication by:
options: Gathering at the leakage field over a discontinuity
Dissolving into the surrounding metal of the solid part
Evaporating off the part surface during the test run
Changing the color of the metal part being inspected
content.explanation: Particles are attracted to and held by the leakage field at a flaw, building up to outline it. The buildup is the indication.
distractors: Particles sit on the surface; they do not dissolve into the metal.
Particles accumulate at the flaw; they do not evaporate.
The indication is a particle buildup, not a change in the metal's color.

content.stem: A discontinuity is most detectable when the magnetic field is:
options: Roughly perpendicular (transverse) to the discontinuity
Running roughly parallel along the discontinuity line
Switched off entirely throughout the whole inspection
Replaced by a focused beam of ordinary visible light
content.explanation: Maximum leakage occurs when the field crosses the flaw at a large angle. A flaw lying parallel to the field causes little leakage and may be missed, which is why two field directions are used.
distractors: A flaw parallel to the field produces little leakage and may be missed.
A field is required; with it off there is no leakage to detect a flaw.
Light does not magnetize the part; a magnetic field is needed.

content.stem: Two magnetizing directions (or multidirectional magnetization) are used because:
options: A single direction can miss flaws parallel to that field
One direction reliably finds every flaw that is present
Two directions are used only to save on inspection time
The particles need both directions in order to glow brightly
content.explanation: Since flaws parallel to the field leak little, the part is magnetized in at least two perpendicular directions so flaws of any orientation are crossed by a field.
distractors: One direction misses flaws aligned with that field, so it cannot find everything.
Using two directions is about coverage of flaw orientations, not speed.
Particle fluorescence depends on the particle type, not the number of directions.

content.stem: MT is classified as a:
options: A surface and near-surface NDT method
A volumetric method reading full thickness
A method intended for nonmagnetic parts
A method based on penetrating radiation
content.explanation: Like PT, MT examines at and just below the surface. It is not a volumetric method like radiography or ultrasonics.
distractors: Volumetric methods examine the full thickness; MT does not.
MT is for ferromagnetic parts, not nonmagnetic ones.
MT uses magnetism and particles, not radiation.

content.stem: An advantage of MT over PT on suitable parts is that MT can:
options: Detect some flaws lying slightly below the surface
Work on aluminum and other fully nonmagnetic metals
Find deep internal voids hidden within the part body
Skip the surface cleaning step before the inspection
content.explanation: MT can reveal some near-surface flaws that PT, a strictly surface method, cannot. It still requires ferromagnetic material and adequate preparation.
distractors: MT cannot work on aluminum, which is nonmagnetic; PT can.
MT does not find deep internal voids; it is surface and near-surface.
MT still needs the surface clean enough for valid results.

content.stem: Compared with PT, a limitation of MT is that it:
options: It works only on ferromagnetic materials
It cannot find any surface-breaking cracks
It needs no electrical or magnetizing power
It requires heavy radiation shielding to use
content.explanation: MT is restricted to ferromagnetic materials. For nonmagnetic metals like aluminum or austenitic stainless, PT is used instead.
distractors: MT readily finds surface cracks; that is a core use.
MT generally needs a magnetizing source, often electrical.
MT uses no ionizing radiation and needs no shielding.

content.stem: Magnetic flux refers to:
options: The magnetic field, drawn as lines of flux in the part
An electric current flowing through the body of the part
The flow of heat passing through the body of the part
A beam of visible light passing through the part itself
content.explanation: Flux is the magnetic field represented as flux lines. Their interruption at a flaw produces the leakage field MT relies on.
distractors: Flux is magnetic, distinct from electric current, though current can create flux.
Flux is a magnetic field, not heat flow.
Flux is magnetic, not light.

content.stem: Magnetic poles are where:
options: Flux leaves and re-enters the part, producing attraction
The part reaching its very hottest local surface temperature
Electric arcs forming across the surface of the part
The part has been painted a clearly different color
content.explanation: At poles, flux exits and re-enters the material. A flaw creates local poles whose leakage field attracts particles.
distractors: Poles are a magnetic feature, not a temperature feature.
Poles are about flux, not electric arcs.
Poles are unrelated to paint.

content.stem: Two like magnetic poles (north and north) will:
options: Repel one another
Attract one another
Cancel each other's magnetism
Generate heat between them
content.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. This basic behavior underlies how leakage poles at a flaw hold particles.
distractors: Unlike poles attract; like poles do not.
Like poles repel; they do not cancel the material's magnetism.
Pole interaction is a force, not a heat source.

content.stem: When current or a magnet is applied to a steel part, the part:
options: Becomes magnetized and carries a field
Melts and deforms from the applied current
Becomes permanently nonmagnetic afterward
Loses every bit of its magnetic flux
content.explanation: Applying a magnetizing force induces a magnetic field in the ferromagnetic part. That field, distorted at flaws, enables detection.
distractors: Magnetizing does not melt the part.
Magnetizing makes a ferromagnetic part carry a field, not become nonmagnetic.
Magnetizing adds flux to the part rather than removing it.

content.stem: A residual magnetic field is the magnetism that:
options: Remains in the part after the force is removed
Exists only while the current is actively flowing
Sits in the air immediately surrounding the part
Comes from the magnetic particles that are used
content.explanation: After magnetizing, ferromagnetic materials retain some field, the residual field. Its strength depends on the material's retentivity and may require demagnetization later.
distractors: Field present only during current is the applied field, not the residual field.
Residual field is in the part, not the surrounding air.
Residual field comes from the part's retained magnetism, not the particles.

content.stem: Retentivity describes a material's ability to:
options: Retain a residual field after magnetizing
Conduct heat through its entire solid body
Resist corrosion across its outer surface
Reflect visible light from its outer surface
content.explanation: High-retentivity materials hold a strong residual field, which makes the residual method possible and often requires demagnetization afterward.
distractors: Retentivity is about retained magnetism, not heat conduction.
Retentivity is unrelated to corrosion resistance.
Retentivity is magnetic, not optical.

content.stem: Magnetic permeability is a measure of how easily a material:
options: Can be magnetized and accept magnetic flux
Conducts an electric current through it
Bends under an applied mechanical load
Melts when heated to a very high temperature
content.explanation: High-permeability materials magnetize easily and carry flux well. Permeability and retentivity together influence how a part behaves in MT.
distractors: Permeability is about accepting magnetic flux, not electrical conduction.
Permeability is magnetic, not a measure of bending.
Permeability is unrelated to melting.

content.stem: In MT, an indication is:
options: The particle buildup held by a leakage field
The acceptance limit set by the specification
The magnetizing current applied in the test
The demagnetizer used after the inspection
content.explanation: An indication is the visible accumulation of particles at a leakage field. It marks a discontinuity or a nonrelevant condition that must then be interpreted.
distractors: An acceptance limit is a criterion, not the particle buildup.
The magnetizing current creates the field; it is not the indication.
The demagnetizer removes residual field; it is not the indication.

content.stem: A discontinuity is:
options: An interruption in the normal structure of the part
A passing inspection result reported after the test
A particular type of magnetic particle being used
A coil that is used to magnetize the part body
content.explanation: A discontinuity is a break in the expected material structure. Whether it is rejectable depends on evaluation against acceptance criteria.
distractors: A discontinuity is a condition in the part, not an inspection outcome.
A discontinuity is not a particle.
A discontinuity is not a piece of equipment.

content.stem: MT sensitivity to subsurface flaws is:
options: Limited to a shallow depth, decreasing with depth
Unlimited and entirely unaffected by the flaw depth
Greatest for the very deepest flaws in the part
Completely independent of the flaw's depth
content.explanation: Leakage at the surface weakens quickly with flaw depth, so MT detects only shallow subsurface flaws, and detectability falls as the flaw lies deeper.
distractors: MT cannot detect flaws at unlimited depth.
Deeper flaws are harder, not easier, to detect.
Detectability does depend on depth.

content.stem: Which material generally cannot be inspected by MT?
options: Austenitic stainless steel
Ordinary low-carbon steel
Common gray cast iron alloy
Typical low-alloy steel grade
content.explanation: Austenitic stainless is essentially nonmagnetic, so MT does not work on it. Carbon steel, cast iron, and low-alloy steel are ferromagnetic and suit MT.
distractors: Carbon steel is ferromagnetic and is a typical MT material.
Cast iron is ferromagnetic and can be inspected by MT.
Low-alloy steel is ferromagnetic and is readily inspected by MT.

content.stem: Before MT, the surface generally must be:
options: Clean enough for particles to move and indications to show
Coated in a thick layer of protective paint and primer
Heavily oiled all over just before the inspection begins
Wetted down with plenty of water for the dry powder method
content.explanation: Dirt, heavy paint, or scale can block particle movement and hide indications, so the surface is prepared appropriately for the method used.
distractors: Thick paint can mask indications and impede particle mobility.
Heavy oil interferes with particle mobility and visibility.
Dry-method inspection needs a dry surface, not a wet one.

content.stem: In MT, the magnetic field that matters is:
options: Inside and at the surface of the part inspected
Only in the air immediately around the part
Only within the power supply cord and its cable
Only inside the magnetic particles themselves
content.explanation: The part is magnetized so flux runs through it; leakage at the surface is what reveals flaws. The field is in the part, not merely in the surroundings.
distractors: The detecting field is in the part and at its surface, not just in the air.
The power cord is not where the inspection field acts.
Particles respond to the part's leakage field; the field is not in the particles.

content.stem: A tight surface crack lying across the field lines will:
options: Produce a strong leakage field and a clear indication
Produce no leakage field at all at the part surface
Conduct the magnetizing current harmlessly away from it
Demagnetize the part that is being inspected here
content.explanation: A crack transverse to the field strongly interrupts the flux, giving a strong leakage field and a sharp particle indication.
distractors: A transverse crack produces strong, not zero, leakage.
A crack distorts flux; it does not carry current away.
A crack does not demagnetize the part.

content.stem: A crack lying parallel to the field lines is likely to:
options: Produce little leakage and may be missed
Always give the strongest indication seen
Heat the part along its length
Reverse the direction of the field
content.explanation: Flux runs along a parallel crack with little interruption, so leakage is weak and the flaw may not show. This is why a second perpendicular direction is required.
distractors: A parallel crack gives weak, not the strongest, leakage.
A parallel crack does not heat the part.
A parallel crack does not reverse the magnetic field.

content.stem: For a nonmagnetic aluminum part needing surface flaw detection, the appropriate method is:
options: PT, because MT cannot magnetize aluminum
MT, because it is simply the faster method
MT, because aluminum is a ferromagnetic metal
Neither method works on any kind of metal
content.explanation: Aluminum is nonmagnetic, so MT cannot be used; liquid penetrant testing is the surface method of choice for it.
distractors: Speed does not matter if MT cannot magnetize the material.
Aluminum is not ferromagnetic.
Both methods work on appropriate metals; PT suits aluminum.

content.stem: A Level I in MT is generally qualified to:
options: Perform the magnetizing and recording under direction
Write the acceptance criteria for the part being tested
Approve the written inspection procedures that are used
Certify other inspectors working in the method
content.explanation: A Level I performs the test and records results to a written procedure under higher-level direction. Setting criteria and approving procedures are higher-level functions.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from codes and higher-level personnel.
Approving procedures is a Level III responsibility.
Certifying inspectors is not a Level I function.

content.stem: Final evaluation of an indication against acceptance criteria is normally done by:
options: A Level II or III inspector
A Level I inspector only
The machine operator on shift
The magnetic particle supplier
content.explanation: Performing and recording is Level I work; interpreting and evaluating indications against the acceptance standard is generally a Level II or higher responsibility.
distractors: Evaluation to acceptance criteria is above the Level I scope.
The machine operator does not evaluate NDT indications.
The particle supplier provides materials, not evaluations.

content.stem: MT is widely used on steel parts because it:
options: Quickly reveals surface flaws and is relatively simple
Finds deep internal voids hidden within the part body
Works on essentially any kind of material there is
Needs no magnetic field at all in order to function well
content.explanation: On ferromagnetic parts, MT is fast, sensitive to surface and near-surface flaws, and relatively simple, which makes it common in many industries.
distractors: MT does not find deep internal voids.
MT works only on ferromagnetic materials.
MT requires a magnetic field to function.

content.stem: The strength of a leakage field at a flaw depends partly on:
options: Flaw orientation, depth, and the applied field strength
Only the ambient temperature of the room around it
The standing height of the inspector who is present today
The painted surface color of the part being tested
content.explanation: Leakage is stronger for flaws transverse to the field, nearer the surface, and when the magnetizing field is adequate. Weak fields or poor orientation reduce indications.
distractors: Room temperature is not the main driver of leakage strength.
Inspector height is irrelevant.
Part color does not affect the leakage field.

content.stem: Particles outline a flaw because they:
options: Bridge across the leakage field and gather at the flaw
Chemically etch into the metal right at the flaw opening
Melt and then flow down into the open crack itself
Paint a colored layer across the whole part surface
content.explanation: Held by the north and south leakage poles, particles bridge the gap and pile up along the flaw, making it visible.
distractors: Particles do not etch the metal.
Particles accumulate on the surface; they do not melt into the crack.
Particles form a magnetic indication, not a paint coat.

content.stem: To perform MT, the part must be:
options: Magnetized by a suitable source during the process
Heated until the whole part visibly glows red hot
Soaked first in a liquid penetrant bath beforehand
Coated with a dry developer powder layer first
content.explanation: A magnetizing source (yoke, prods, coil, or current) establishes the field in the part so flaws can leak and hold particles.
distractors: Parts are not heated to red heat for MT.
Penetrant soaking is the PT method, not MT.
Developer is a PT material, not used to magnetize for MT.

content.stem: Typical discontinuities found by MT include:
options: Surface and near-surface cracks, seams, and laps in steel
Only deep internal voids located within the part body
Flaws contained entirely within molded plastic parts
Subsurface flaws located at essentially any depth at all
content.explanation: MT readily reveals surface and shallow subsurface cracks, seams, laps, and similar flaws in ferromagnetic parts.
distractors: MT does not find deep internal voids.
Plastics are nonmagnetic and unsuitable for MT.
MT detects only shallow subsurface flaws, not at any depth.

content.stem: Applying far more magnetizing field than needed can:
options: Cause heavy background that hides relevant indications
Always improve the detection of every single flaw there
Make the steel part become permanently nonmagnetic
Remove the need to apply any particles at all
content.explanation: Over-magnetizing can furnish heavy nonrelevant background and particle adherence that mask real indications, so field strength is controlled to an appropriate level.
distractors: More field is not always better; excess causes masking background.
Strong field does not make steel nonmagnetic.
Particles are still required to see indications.

content.stem: The magnetic field used in MT is most commonly produced by:
options: Electric current or a magnet such as a yoke
A radioactive source held close to the part
Ultrasound transmitted into the part body
Heat applied across the surface of the part
content.explanation: Fields are produced by passing current through the part or a conductor, or by a yoke or permanent magnet. Radiation, ultrasound, and heat are other methods entirely.
distractors: Radioactive sources belong to radiography, not MT.
Ultrasound is a different method.
Heat does not magnetize the part for MT.

content.stem: MT shows where particles gather, but deciding accept or reject requires:
options: Evaluating the indication against acceptance criteria
Nothing further at all beyond just seeing the indication
Only counting up the number of particles present
Weighing the part carefully on an accurate scale
content.explanation: An indication must be interpreted and evaluated against the acceptance standard, a step beyond simply seeing the particle buildup, and generally a higher-level task.
distractors: An indication alone does not decide acceptance; evaluation is needed.
Counting particles is not how acceptance is judged.
Part weight is unrelated to evaluating an indication.

content.stem: Magnetic particles are available as:
options: Dry powders and wet liquid suspensions
Only liquids and never as a dry powder
Only gases sprayed onto the surface
Only solids fused onto the part surface
content.explanation: Particles come as dry powders or as wet suspensions (in water or oil carrier). Each suits different applications, covered later.
distractors: Wet suspensions are one form, but dry powders also exist.
Particles are not used as gases.
Particles are applied loosely, not fused to the part.

content.stem: Magnetic particles can be:
options: Visible in white light or fluorescent under UV-A
Only ever completely invisible to the unaided eye
Only radioactive sources of light of their own
Only a single fixed magnetic north pole on each
content.explanation: Visible particles are read under white light by color contrast; fluorescent particles glow under UV-A for higher sensitivity. The choice depends on the inspection.
distractors: Particles are made to be seen, not invisible.
Particles are not radioactive.
Particles are magnetic but are not a single pole; they bridge leakage fields.

content.stem: MT involves hazards mainly from:
options: Electrical equipment and, with prods, possible arcing
Ionizing radiation given off by the testing unit itself
High explosives used during the testing process
Pressurized gas as the only hazard of any kind
content.explanation: Magnetizing equipment carries electrical hazards, and prods can arc or burn the surface. MT does not involve ionizing radiation.
distractors: MT does not use ionizing radiation.
MT does not involve high explosives.
Pressurized gas is not the primary MT hazard.

content.stem: Which statement about MT is correct?
options: It finds surface and near-surface flaws in steel via flux leakage
It reaches deep internal voids throughout the full part thickness
It works directly on aluminum and on other fully nonmagnetic metals
It needs no magnetic field at all in order to find any flaws
content.explanation: MT uses flux leakage to reveal surface and shallow subsurface flaws in ferromagnetic materials. It does not find deep flaws, does not work on aluminum, and requires a magnetic field.
distractors: MT does not detect deep internal voids.
Aluminum is nonmagnetic and unsuitable for MT.
A magnetic field is essential to MT.

content.stem: The two basic field directions in MT are:
options: Circular and longitudinal fields
Plain up-and-down vertical directions
Hot and cold temperature states
Wet and dry particle media types
content.explanation: Magnetization is either circular (field around the part) or longitudinal (field along the part's length). Each finds flaws of a particular orientation.
distractors: Up and down do not describe MT field directions.
Hot and cold are temperatures, not field directions.
Wet and dry describe particle media, not field direction.

content.stem: Circular magnetization produces a field that best detects:
options: Longitudinal (axial) discontinuities
Transverse-only surface discontinuities
Deep subsurface internal voids only
No discontinuities of any kind
content.explanation: A circular field runs around the part, crossing flaws that run lengthwise (axially), so circular magnetization finds longitudinal flaws.
distractors: Transverse flaws are best found by longitudinal magnetization, not circular.
Circular magnetization targets surface-breaking flaw orientation, not deep voids.
Circular magnetization does detect flaws of the right orientation.

content.stem: Longitudinal magnetization produces a field that best detects:
options: Transverse (circumferential) discontinuities
Longitudinal axial discontinuities only
Deep internal voids inside the whole part body
No discontinuities of any kind at all
content.explanation: A longitudinal field runs along the part's length, crossing flaws oriented across the part, so it finds transverse flaws.
distractors: Longitudinal flaws are best found by circular magnetization.
Longitudinal magnetization targets surface flaw orientation, not deep voids.
It does detect transverse flaws.

content.stem: The governing rule for choosing a magnetizing direction is that the field should be:
options: Perpendicular to the expected discontinuity
Running parallel to the expected discontinuity
Switched off during the whole inspection
Pointed directly toward the inspector
content.explanation: Maximum leakage occurs when the field crosses the flaw. The method is chosen so the field is roughly perpendicular to the flaws being sought.
distractors: A field parallel to the flaw gives little leakage and misses it.
The field must be present during the continuous method inspection.
Field direction is about flaw orientation, not pointing at the inspector.

content.stem: A magnetic yoke produces a:
options: A longitudinal field between its two poles
A circular field around the entire part
A beam of deeply penetrating radiation
A thin film of applied liquid penetrant dye
content.explanation: A yoke placed on the surface sets up a longitudinal field between its legs, good for finding flaws transverse to a line between the poles.
distractors: A yoke produces a longitudinal, not circular, field.
A yoke is magnetic, not a radiation source.
A yoke magnetizes; it does not apply penetrant.

content.stem: Prods are used to produce a:
options: A circular field between the prod tips
A longitudinal field along the whole part
A magnetic field with no current flowing
A beam of ultraviolet (UV-A) light
content.explanation: Prods pass current through a local area of the part, creating a circular field around the current path between the tips, useful for welds and large surfaces.
distractors: Prods give a local circular field, not a whole-part longitudinal field.
Prods rely on current passing through the part.
Prods magnetize; they do not produce UV-A light.

content.stem: A current-carrying coil (solenoid) around a part produces a:
options: A longitudinal field along the part axis
A circular field around the whole part body
No field anywhere within the part
A field only within the coil wire itself
content.explanation: Placing the part in or against a coil induces a longitudinal field along its length, finding transverse flaws. The coil is an indirect magnetization method.
distractors: A coil gives a longitudinal, not circular, field in the part.
A coil with current does produce a field.
The coil's field magnetizes the part, not only the wire.

content.stem: A central conductor passed through a hollow part produces a:
options: A circular field with no current through the part
A longitudinal field along the whole part length
A field present only in the nearby air
No magnetization of the part at all anywhere on it
content.explanation: Current through a conductor threaded inside a ring or tube creates a circular field in the surrounding part, inspecting inner and outer surfaces without current through the part itself.
distractors: A central conductor gives a circular, not longitudinal, field.
It magnetizes the surrounding part, not only the air.
It does magnetize the part circularly.

content.stem: A head shot (direct current through a part on a bench) produces a:
options: A circular field around the part
A longitudinal field along the part
A penetrating radiation field
A field only once it is demagnetized
content.explanation: Clamping a part between the contact heads and passing current through it creates a circular field around the part, finding longitudinal flaws.
distractors: A head shot gives a circular, not longitudinal, field.
A head shot is magnetic, not radiation.
A field is produced during magnetizing, not when demagnetized.

content.stem: Direct magnetization means:
options: Current is passed through the part itself
A field is induced with no current in the part
No current is used at any point at all
The part is heated up during the test
content.explanation: Direct magnetization passes current through the part (head shot, prods), creating a circular field. Indirect magnetization (coil, yoke, central conductor) induces a field without current through the part.
distractors: Inducing a field without current in the part is indirect magnetization.
Direct magnetization does use current, through the part.
Direct magnetization is about current path, not heating.

content.stem: Which is an indirect magnetization technique?
options: A coil placed around the part
A head shot through the part
Prods touching the part surface
Direct contact current flow
content.explanation: A coil induces a longitudinal field without passing current through the part, making it indirect. Head shots and prods pass current through the part and are direct.
distractors: A head shot passes current through the part and is direct.
Prods pass current through the part and are direct.
Direct contact current is, by definition, direct magnetization.

content.stem: For inspecting a weld for cracks running along its length, a common approach is:
options: Prods or a yoke set to cross the weld with the field
A field running parallel along the entire weld length
No magnetization of the weld area at all
Only demagnetization of the weld region
content.explanation: Longitudinal weld cracks are found by a field crossing them. Prods or a yoke are positioned so the field runs across the weld, and a second orientation covers transverse flaws.
distractors: A field parallel to the cracks gives little leakage.
Magnetization is required to detect the flaws.
Demagnetization alone does not detect flaws.

content.stem: To cover flaws of all orientations on a shaft, the part is typically magnetized:
options: Circularly and longitudinally, in two directions
In the circular direction only, just once
In the longitudinal direction only, one single time
Once in any single chosen direction
content.explanation: A circular shot finds longitudinal flaws and a longitudinal shot finds transverse flaws, so both are used (or multidirectional magnetization) for full coverage.
distractors: Circular only would miss transverse flaws.
Longitudinal only would miss longitudinal flaws.
A single arbitrary direction leaves some flaw orientations uncovered.

content.stem: An advantage of the yoke is that it is:
options: Portable and needs no current through the part
Usable only on a large fixed shop bench
A source of deeply penetrating radiation
Able to find deep internal voids inside parts
content.explanation: Yokes are portable, magnetize without passing current through the part (reducing arc/burn risk), and are common for field and weld inspection.
distractors: Yokes are portable handheld tools, not bench-only.
Yokes are magnetic, not radiation sources.
Yokes find surface and near-surface flaws, not deep voids.

content.stem: A drawback of prods is the risk of:
options: Arc strikes or burns where the tips touch the part
Producing a longitudinal field along the whole part
Needing no current at all in order to operate
Working only on nonmagnetic aluminum parts
content.explanation: Because current passes through the prod tips, poor contact can arc and burn the surface. Many specifications restrict prods on critical or finished surfaces for this reason.
distractors: Prods produce a circular field; that is their function, not a drawback.
Prods do require current; that is the source of the arc risk.
Prods are used on ferromagnetic parts, not aluminum.

content.stem: A benefit of the central conductor technique is that it:
options: Inspects inner and outer surfaces with no current in the part
Heats the part up noticeably during the entire inspection run
Requires separate prods to carry all of the current
Detects only transverse flaws in the part body
content.explanation: Threading a conductor through a ring or tube magnetizes the part circularly without passing current through it, avoiding contact burns and reaching the bore.
distractors: The central conductor does not heat the part.
It replaces prods rather than requiring them.
Circular magnetization finds longitudinal flaws, not transverse.

content.stem: A part placed in a coil is being magnetized to find:
options: Transverse flaws in the part
Longitudinal flaws in the part
No flaws in the part at all
Only deep subsurface voids
content.explanation: The coil's longitudinal field crosses transverse flaws, so the coil shot targets flaws oriented across the part.
distractors: Longitudinal flaws are found by circular magnetization.
The coil does magnetize and detect appropriately oriented flaws.
The coil targets surface flaw orientation, not deep voids.

content.stem: When magnetizing a part in a coil, the part's length-to-diameter ratio matters because it affects:
options: The effective field strength developed in the part
The color of the magnetic particles being applied here
The level of the white viewing light in use
The overall weight of the whole part
content.explanation: The L/D ratio influences how effectively the coil magnetizes the part, which is why procedures account for it when setting coil current. The Level I follows the procedure values.
distractors: L/D ratio does not change particle color.
L/D ratio is unrelated to white light level.
L/D ratio does not change the part's weight.

content.stem: Prod spacing is controlled because it affects:
options: The field strength and coverage between the tips
The particular type of magnetic particles being used
The wavelength of the UV-A viewing light
The painted color of the tested part
content.explanation: The distance between prods affects the field in the area inspected, so procedures specify a spacing range. Too far apart weakens the field; too close limits coverage.
distractors: Prod spacing does not change the particle type.
Prod spacing is unrelated to UV-A wavelength.
Prod spacing does not change part color.

content.stem: Multidirectional magnetization equipment is designed to:
options: Establish fields in several directions in rapid sequence
Operate using no magnetizing current at all in the unit
Detect only one single flaw orientation each time
Take the place of the magnetic particles entirely
content.explanation: Multidirectional units rapidly alternate field directions so flaws of multiple orientations are revealed in one operation, when qualified for the part.
distractors: Multidirectional magnetization uses current to establish fields.
Its purpose is to cover multiple orientations, not one.
Particles are still required to see indications.

content.stem: Knowing the magnetization method tells the technician:
options: Which flaw orientations that shot will best reveal
The full acceptance criteria written for the part
The heat treatment given to the steel part
The radiographic technique that should be used
content.explanation: Because circular and longitudinal fields detect different flaw orientations, the method indicates which flaws a given shot will find, guiding the need for a second direction.
distractors: Acceptance criteria come from the specification, not the method alone.
Heat treatment is unrelated to the magnetization method.
Radiographic technique is a different method.

content.stem: Both legs of a yoke should contact the surface because:
options: Good contact is needed to carry the field into the part
It simply makes the whole bench setup look much neater overall
It helps to cool the hot part down faster
It cleans the surface of the part at the same time
content.explanation: The yoke's field passes into the part through its legs, so firm contact at both feet is needed for an effective field in the inspection area.
distractors: Contact is about field transfer, not appearance.
Yoke contact does not cool the part.
The yoke magnetizes; it does not clean the surface.

content.stem: To find flaws of different orientations with a yoke, the technician:
options: Rotates the yoke and re-inspects perpendicular to the first
Uses only one single fixed field orientation the whole time
Increases the size of the magnetic particles used
Turns the magnetic field off completely
content.explanation: Because a yoke field is directional, the yoke is repositioned about 90 degrees and the area re-inspected so flaws of the other orientation are crossed by the field.
distractors: A single orientation misses flaws aligned with that field.
Particle size is not how orientation coverage is achieved.
The field must be on to detect flaws.

content.stem: An advantage of circular magnetization is that it generally:
options: Confines the field within the part with no external poles
Creates strong external magnetic poles at both ends of the part
Requires a coil in order to work at all
Detects transverse flaws best of all
content.explanation: A circular field largely stays within the part, so there are no strong external poles. This also means a part can hold a circular residual field that is harder to detect externally.
distractors: Circular magnetization produces few external poles, not strong ones.
Circular magnetization can be made by head shots or conductors, not only coils.
Circular magnetization finds longitudinal flaws, not transverse.

content.stem: Longitudinal magnetization tends to create:
options: External north and south poles at the ends of the part
No magnetic field present anywhere in the whole part at all
A circular field running around the part
Heat building up at the center of the part
content.explanation: A longitudinal field exits at the part ends as external poles. These poles can attract particles and produce nonrelevant end indications to be recognized.
distractors: Longitudinal magnetization does produce a field.
It produces a longitudinal, not circular, field.
It is a magnetic effect, not heating.

content.stem: Selecting the magnetization technique depends on:
options: Part shape, size, and the flaw orientations of concern
The particular day of the working week
The standing height of the inspector who is present today
Only the painted outer color of the part
content.explanation: Geometry, accessibility, and which flaw orientations matter drive the choice among yoke, prods, coil, central conductor, and head shot.
distractors: The day of the week is irrelevant.
Inspector height is irrelevant.
Particle color is a separate choice from magnetization technique.

content.stem: A bearing ring is best magnetized for inner and outer surface flaws using a:
options: A central conductor through the ring
A single prod placed on one spot
A yoke held on just one small spot
A coil only, meant for circular flaws
content.explanation: Threading a central conductor through the ring creates a circular field around the whole circumference, inspecting both bore and outer surface in one operation.
distractors: A single prod covers only a small local area, not the whole ring.
A yoke on one spot covers a limited area and direction.
A coil gives a longitudinal field, not the circular field a central conductor provides.

content.stem: Prods are often chosen for:
options: Large castings and weldments needing local circular fields
Tiny precision bearings and other very small parts
Nonmagnetic parts such as aluminum, brass, or copper alloy
Taking the place of the magnetic particles entirely
content.explanation: Prods apply a local circular field and are practical on large weldments and castings, moving from area to area, where restrictions on arc strikes allow.
distractors: Tiny precision parts are usually handled by bench or central-conductor methods, not prods.
Prods do not work on nonmagnetic parts.
Prods magnetize; they do not replace particles.

content.stem: An AC yoke is generally best for:
options: Surface-breaking discontinuities
Deep subsurface internal flaws only
Nonmagnetic parts like aluminum alloy
Demagnetizing the finished part only
content.explanation: AC concentrates the field near the surface (skin effect), making an AC yoke well suited to surface flaws. A DC yoke reaches slightly deeper for near-surface flaws.
distractors: Deep subsurface flaws favor DC, and even then only shallow depths.
Yokes work on ferromagnetic, not nonmagnetic, parts.
An AC yoke magnetizes for inspection, not only demagnetizing.

content.stem: After setting up a magnetization shot, the technician verifies the field is adequate using:
options: A field indicator such as a pie gauge or shim
A thermometer reading the part surface temperature
A tape measure checking part length
A simple stopwatch used on its own
content.explanation: Field indicators confirm a field of sufficient strength and correct direction is present at the surface before relying on the shot. These are covered with equipment.
distractors: A thermometer measures temperature, not field adequacy.
A tape measure checks dimensions, not the field.
A stopwatch times events; it does not confirm the field.

content.stem: To reduce arc and burn risk in direct (contact) magnetization, the technician should ensure:
options: Good clean contact and current applied per procedure
Loose, dirty contacts at the prod tips
The maximum possible current used every time
Current applied while the whole part is still solvent-wet
content.explanation: Clean, firm contacts and controlled current reduce arcing and overheating at the contact points. Poor contact and excessive current increase burn risk.
distractors: Loose, dirty contacts increase arcing and burns.
Excessive current raises overheating and burn risk.
Applying current to a solvent-wet part adds hazards rather than reducing them.

content.stem: If transverse cracks are the concern on a long bar, the technician would magnetize it:
options: Longitudinally, for example inside a coil
Circularly, using a single head shot
Not magnetized in any way at all
Only after it has first been demagnetized
content.explanation: Transverse cracks are crossed by a longitudinal field, so a coil (or other longitudinal method) is selected for them.
distractors: A circular head shot targets longitudinal flaws, not transverse.
Magnetization is needed to detect the cracks.
Demagnetizing removes field; it does not detect flaws.

content.stem: When using a central conductor on a tube, indications can appear on:
options: Both the inner bore and the outer surface
Only on the outer surface of the whole part
Only inside the central conductor bar
On neither surface of the part at all
content.explanation: The circular field surrounds the conductor and threads through the tube wall, so flaws on both the bore and the outer surface can produce indications.
distractors: Indications are not limited to the outer surface.
Indications form on the part, not inside the conductor.
Appropriately oriented flaws on both surfaces can show.

content.stem: In choosing and setting up magnetization, the Level I technician:
options: Follows the written procedure for method, direction, and current
Invents a brand-new inspection technique for every single part used
Sets the formal acceptance limits for each part himself
Approves the written inspection procedure for use
content.explanation: The procedure specifies the method, directions, and current. The Level I performs the setup accordingly and records it, leaving criteria and approvals to higher levels.
distractors: The technique is specified, not invented per part.
Acceptance limits are set above the Level I.
Procedure approval is a Level III function.

content.stem: On a large surface inspected with a yoke, overlapping the inspection areas helps:
options: Ensure full coverage with adequate field everywhere
Save magnetic particles during the whole inspection
Heat the surface of the part evenly all over
Avoid demagnetizing the finished part
content.explanation: Because the yoke field is strongest between and near the legs, areas are overlapped so every location receives an adequate field and no strip is left uninspected.
distractors: Overlap is about coverage, not saving particles.
Overlap does not relate to heating the surface.
Overlap is about coverage, not demagnetization.

content.stem: Which pairing is correct?
options: Circular fields find longitudinal flaws; longitudinal find transverse
Circular fields always find transverse flaws in the part being tested
Longitudinal fields find only longitudinal flaws in the tested part
Field direction does not matter at all for finding the flaws
content.explanation: A circular field crosses and reveals longitudinal flaws; a longitudinal field crosses and reveals transverse flaws. Two directions cover all orientations.
distractors: Circular fields find longitudinal flaws, not transverse.
Longitudinal fields find transverse flaws, not longitudinal.
Field direction is central to which flaws are found.

content.stem: In MT, the magnetic field is created by:
options: Electric current or a permanent magnet
Heat applied directly to the whole part
Bright light shined on the part
Sound waves sent into the part
content.explanation: Passing current through the part or a conductor, or using a magnet, establishes the magnetic field. The amount of current relates to the field strength.
distractors: Heat does not create the magnetizing field.
Light does not magnetize the part.
Sound does not create the magnetic field.

content.stem: Alternating current (AC) is best for detecting:
options: Surface-breaking discontinuities
Deep subsurface internal flaws only
Flaws found in aluminum parts
Internal voids inside the part
content.explanation: AC concentrates the field near the surface due to the skin effect, giving good surface sensitivity but little subsurface reach.
distractors: Deep subsurface flaws favor direct current, not AC.
AC still requires a ferromagnetic material; aluminum is unsuitable.
AC does not reach internal voids.

content.stem: The skin effect with AC means the field is:
options: Concentrated near the surface of the part
Strongest deep inside the part body
Completely absent at the part surface itself
Uniform through the whole thickness
content.explanation: AC pushes the magnetic field toward the surface, which is why AC excels at surface flaws and is poor for subsurface ones.
distractors: AC is weakest, not strongest, deep inside.
AC concentrates the field at the surface, not away from it.
AC does not distribute the field uniformly through the thickness.

content.stem: Direct current (DC) or full-wave rectified current is preferred when seeking:
options: Slightly subsurface (near-surface) discontinuities
Only flaws lying right at the part surface
Flaws found in nonmagnetic aluminum parts
Deep internal voids located at almost any depth at all
content.explanation: DC penetrates deeper than AC, so it reaches shallow subsurface flaws. Even so, MT subsurface sensitivity is limited to shallow depths.
distractors: AC, not DC, is the better choice purely for surface flaws.
DC still requires ferromagnetic material.
MT cannot reach deep internal voids regardless of current type.

content.stem: Half-wave rectified DC (HWDC) is often used with dry powder because it:
options: Pulsates, aiding dry particle mobility, and penetrates well
Cannot magnetize the steel part at all anyway
Works only on nonmagnetic aluminum parts instead
Provides no useful depth penetration into the steel part at all
content.explanation: The pulsating HWDC current helps dry particles move and orient toward leakage fields, and it penetrates better than AC, which suits castings and rough surfaces.
distractors: HWDC does magnetize steel.
HWDC is for ferromagnetic parts, not aluminum.
HWDC provides good penetration, not none.

content.stem: One advantage of AC is that it:
options: Makes demagnetization relatively easy
Penetrates the deepest of any current
Removes the need to use particles
Works on nonmagnetic parts too
content.explanation: The reversing nature of AC aids demagnetization, since AC fields can be reduced through reversing cycles. AC does not penetrate deeply.
distractors: AC penetrates the least, not the most.
Particles are still needed with AC.
AC works on ferromagnetic parts only.

content.stem: Field strength in the part is most directly related to:
options: The magnitude of the magnetizing current
The color of the magnetic particles used
The level of the white viewing light
The humidity level in the room
content.explanation: More magnetizing current generally produces a stronger field, which is why procedures specify current values. Too little under-magnetizes; too much causes background.
distractors: Particle color does not set field strength.
White light level is a viewing condition, not field strength.
Room humidity does not set the field strength.

content.stem: The right-hand rule relates the direction of current to the direction of the:
options: The circular magnetic field around the conductor
The color of the magnetic particles being applied
The level of the white viewing light
The temperature of the tested part
content.explanation: For current along a conductor, the magnetic field circles it in a direction given by the right-hand rule. This is the circular field used in direct magnetization.
distractors: The rule concerns field direction, not particle color.
The rule is about magnetic field direction, not light.
The rule does not concern temperature.

content.stem: If magnetizing current is too low:
options: The field may be too weak to show flaws
The background is always heavy and dark
The part overheats from the current
Demagnetization later fails
content.explanation: An inadequate field produces weak leakage, so real flaws may not form clear indications. Current is set to the procedure level.
distractors: Heavy background is associated with excessive, not low, current.
Low current does not overheat the part.
Low magnetizing current does not by itself cause demagnetization to fail.

content.stem: If magnetizing current is far too high:
options: Excess background can mask real indications
Flaws always become clearer and easier to see
The steel part becomes fully nonmagnetic
No magnetic field forms in the part at all
content.explanation: Over-magnetizing produces heavy nonrelevant background and particle adherence that can hide genuine indications, so current is controlled.
distractors: Excess current can obscure, not clarify, flaws.
Excess current does not make steel nonmagnetic.
Excess current produces a strong field, not none.

content.stem: The Level I sets magnetizing current based on:
options: The written procedure for the part and technique
A random guess made on the spot each time
The brand of magnetic particles being used today
The level of the ambient room light
content.explanation: Current values come from the procedure, which accounts for part size, geometry, and technique. The Level I applies and records them.
distractors: Current is specified, not guessed.
Particle brand does not set magnetizing current.
Ambient light is a viewing condition, not a current setting.

content.stem: Comparing AC and DC at the same current, DC generally provides:
options: Greater depth of field penetration
Better surface-only concentration
No magnetic field forming at all
A field only in aluminum parts alone
content.explanation: DC penetrates deeper than AC, while AC concentrates at the surface. The choice depends on whether surface or near-surface flaws are sought.
distractors: Surface-only concentration is the AC characteristic.
DC does produce a field.
DC magnetizes ferromagnetic parts, not aluminum.

content.stem: Rectified current in MT refers to:
options: AC converted toward DC, half-wave or full-wave
A current that flows with no direction
A particular type of magnetic particle product
A demagnetizing field and nothing more
content.explanation: Rectifiers convert AC into half-wave or full-wave rectified current, giving DC-like penetration, sometimes with a useful pulsating quality for dry particles.
distractors: Rectified current has a direction; that is the point of rectifying.
Rectified current is an electrical form, not a particle.
Rectified current is used to magnetize for inspection, not only to demagnetize.

content.stem: Passing current directly through a part produces a field that is:
options: Circular around the current path
Longitudinal along the whole part
Absent, with no field formed at all
Present only outside the part body
content.explanation: Direct current through the part creates a circular field around the current path, which finds longitudinal flaws.
distractors: Direct contact current gives a circular, not longitudinal, field.
A field is produced when current flows.
The circular field is in and around the part, not only external.

content.stem: Current in a coil around the part produces a field that is:
options: Longitudinal along the part axis
Circular around the whole part body
Absent, with no field formed at all
Present only within the coil wire
content.explanation: Coil current induces a longitudinal field along the part, which finds transverse flaws.
distractors: A coil gives a longitudinal, not circular, field in the part.
A field is produced when coil current flows.
The coil magnetizes the part, not only the coil wire.

content.stem: Procedures sometimes set head-shot current as amperes per inch of part diameter. The Level I should:
options: Apply the procedure value for the part size
Ignore the overall size of the part
Always use the maximum current that is available
Use one fixed current for every part
content.explanation: The required current scales with part size, so the technician computes or reads the value from the procedure for the specific part rather than using a fixed amount.
distractors: Part size affects the required current and cannot be ignored.
Maximum current can over-magnetize and cause background.
A single fixed current does not suit parts of different sizes.

content.stem: Rather than assume the field is adequate, the technician should:
options: Verify it with a field indicator at the surface
Trust the current meter reading alone, on its own
Skip the verification step altogether
Estimate it from the part's color
content.explanation: Field indicators such as a pie gauge, QQI/shim, or gauss meter confirm an adequate field of the right direction is actually present at the surface.
distractors: A current meter alone does not confirm the surface field direction and adequacy.
Verification is part of a valid setup, not skipped.
Part color does not indicate field adequacy.

content.stem: AC also aids inspection by giving particles:
options: Added mobility from the alternating field
No movement at all across the surface
A permanent magnet coating left on each one
A bright fluorescent glow under UV
content.explanation: The alternating field imparts some vibration and mobility to particles, helping them move to leakage fields. Glow comes from fluorescent dye, not the current.
distractors: AC adds mobility rather than stopping movement.
AC does not coat particles with a permanent magnet.
Fluorescence comes from particle type, not the current.

content.stem: Some longitudinal magnetizing circuits use a quick-break feature to:
options: Improve detection near the ends of the part
Heat the part up during the shot
Demagnetize the part during the shot
Change the color of the magnetic particles used
content.explanation: A quick-break (rapid interruption) can enhance the field distribution and improve indications near part ends in some longitudinal setups. The Level I uses equipment as the procedure directs.
distractors: Quick-break is a field effect, not a heating function.
It is part of magnetizing, not demagnetizing during the shot.
It does not change particle color.

content.stem: Compared with AC, DC magnetization tends to leave:
options: A stronger residual field, often needing full demagnetization
No residual field left anywhere in the whole part afterward at all
A field only in the air surrounding the tested part
A part left completely nonmagnetic after the test
content.explanation: DC typically produces a stronger, deeper residual field than AC, so DC-magnetized parts often require careful demagnetization.
distractors: DC leaves a residual field rather than none.
The residual field is in the part, not only the air.
Magnetization does not make the part nonmagnetic.

content.stem: Choosing between AC and DC current depends mainly on:
options: Whether flaws are at the surface or slightly subsurface
The inspector's own personal preference for a given color
The particular time of the working day
The brand name of the particle carrier
content.explanation: Surface flaws favor AC; near-surface flaws favor DC. The expected flaw depth drives the current choice within the procedure.
distractors: Color preference does not determine current type.
Time of day is irrelevant.
The particle carrier brand does not set the current type.

content.stem: Reversing the direction of magnetizing current reverses the:
options: The direction of the magnetic field
The color of the magnetic particles
The level of white viewing light
The hardness of the part
content.explanation: Field direction follows current direction. This is used in demagnetization, where current is reversed and reduced step by step.
distractors: Current direction does not change particle color.
Current direction does not change white light level.
Current direction does not change part hardness.

content.stem: Full-wave rectified DC (FWDC) is generally chosen for:
options: Better subsurface sensitivity than AC
Surface-only inspection of the whole part
Use on nonmagnetic aluminum parts only
Demagnetizing the finished part only
content.explanation: FWDC provides smooth DC-like penetration for near-surface flaws, deeper than AC. It is used to magnetize for inspection, not only to demagnetize.
distractors: Surface-only inspection is better served by AC.
FWDC works on ferromagnetic parts, not aluminum.
FWDC magnetizes for inspection, not solely demagnetization.

content.stem: When using the continuous method, the magnetizing current is applied:
options: While the particles are applied and the indication forms
Only after all the magnetic particles have completely dried
Only after the whole part is demagnetized
Never at any point during the inspection itself
content.explanation: In the continuous method the field is on as particles are applied, giving maximum sensitivity. The current duration follows the procedure.
distractors: Particles are applied during the current, not only after drying.
Magnetizing precedes demagnetizing, not the reverse.
The field must be present to form indications in the continuous method.

content.stem: A device that reads magnetic field strength (such as tangential field) is a:
options: A gauss or Hall-effect meter
A radiographic film densitometer
A handheld illuminance light meter
A rotational speed tachometer
content.explanation: A gauss or Hall-effect meter measures field strength, helping confirm adequate magnetization. Densitometers and illuminance meters serve other methods.
distractors: A densitometer measures radiographic film density.
An illuminance meter measures visible light level.
A tachometer measures rotational speed.

content.stem: For a rough casting where dry powder and good particle mobility are wanted, a common choice is:
options: Half-wave rectified DC with dry powder
AC with wet fluorescent in a dark booth
No current applied to the casting
A nonmagnetic setup for the casting
content.explanation: HWDC with dry powder gives strong particle mobility and penetration suited to rough castings, which is a common field and shop combination.
distractors: Wet fluorescent in a booth suits fine surface cracks on smoother parts, not the rough-casting dry-powder case described.
Current is required to magnetize the casting.
A nonmagnetic setup cannot magnetize a ferromagnetic casting.

content.stem: The field strength that matters is the field:
options: In the actual area being inspected
In the power supply unit only itself
In the connecting cable run alone
In the separate demagnetizer unit
content.explanation: Adequate field must exist in the inspection area itself, which is why field indicators are placed there to confirm it.
distractors: The power supply reading is not the same as the field at the surface.
Cable field is not what magnetizes the inspection area.
The demagnetizer is a separate device used later.

content.stem: Very high contact current for too long can:
options: Overheat or burn the contact areas
Cool the whole part down quickly
Demagnetize the whole part fully
Neither help nor harm the part at all
content.explanation: Excessive current and dwell at the contacts can overheat and burn the surface, so current and duration are controlled per procedure.
distractors: High current heats, it does not cool, the contacts.
High magnetizing current does not demagnetize the part.
Overheating is a real harm, not a neutral effect.

content.stem: Heavy particle adherence over the whole surface (furring) usually indicates:
options: Too strong a field for the part
Too weak a field for the part
No field present at all
Exactly the correct field strength
content.explanation: An overly strong field makes particles cling everywhere, furring the surface and masking real indications, so the field is reduced toward the proper level.
distractors: A weak field gives faint indications, not heavy overall furring.
No field would give no particle holding at all.
Furring is a sign of excess field, not correct strength.

content.stem: The magnetizing current and technique used should be:
options: Recorded as part of performing the test
Kept secret and left out of the records
Chosen at random on each occasion
Ignored and left out of it entirely
content.explanation: Process parameters such as current and technique are documented for traceability, which the Level I records as part of the inspection.
distractors: Process parameters are documented, not secret.
Current is specified, not random.
Parameters are recorded, not ignored.

content.stem: The main reason to have both AC and DC available is to:
options: Match the current to surface versus near-surface flaws
Make the whole unit heavier to carry around
Change the color of the magnetic particles
Increase the overall level of the white viewing light used
content.explanation: Offering AC and DC lets the technician select surface concentration (AC) or deeper penetration (DC) as the inspection requires.
distractors: Equipment weight is not the reason for two current types.
Current type does not set particle color.
Current type is unrelated to white light level.

content.stem: Which statement about magnetizing current is correct?
options: AC concentrates at the surface; DC goes deeper; current sets strength
AC always penetrates the very deepest of any magnetizing current used
DC inspects only the surface of the part and goes no deeper
Current type makes no real difference to the depth reached
content.explanation: AC gives surface concentration, DC reaches near-surface flaws, and the current magnitude controls the field. The type is chosen for the flaws sought.
distractors: AC penetrates the least, not the most.
DC penetrates deeper than AC; it is not surface-only.
Current type strongly affects depth of detection.

content.stem: A yoke is a portable device that magnetizes by:
options: Placing two poles on the surface for a longitudinal field
Passing electric current directly through the whole part body
Spraying liquid penetrant onto the part surface
Emitting penetrating radiation toward the part
content.explanation: A yoke sets up a longitudinal field between its legs without passing current through the part, which makes it portable and low-burn-risk.
distractors: A yoke induces a field; it does not pass current through the part.
A yoke magnetizes; it does not spray penetrant.
A yoke is magnetic, not a radiation source.

content.stem: Yokes are available as:
options: AC, DC, and permanent-magnet types
Only AC-powered yoke types alone
Only radioactive source-based types
Only nonmagnetic material types
content.explanation: Yokes come in AC, DC (electromagnetic), and permanent-magnet forms. AC suits surface flaws; DC reaches slightly deeper.
distractors: Yokes are not limited to AC; DC and permanent-magnet types exist.
Yokes are not radioactive.
A yoke must be magnetic to function.

content.stem: A common functional check of a yoke is its lifting power, typically verified against:
options: A specified test weight at maximum pole spacing
The painted outer color of the part
The temperature of the whole room
The brand name of the magnetic particles being used
content.explanation: Yoke performance is checked by lifting a specified weight at maximum leg spacing (commonly about 10 lb for AC and 40 lb for DC). This lift check appears in MT specifications such as ASTM E1444/E709 and ASME Section V, and the exact weight and wording vary by document and revision, so confirm against the governing specification.
distractors: Part color does not verify yoke lifting power.
Room temperature is not the lift-check criterion.
Particle brand is unrelated to the yoke lift check.

content.stem: A stationary horizontal wet bench typically provides:
options: Head and tail contacts, a coil, and a particle bath
Only a single handheld magnetic yoke
Only an ultraviolet (UV) viewing lamp
Radiation shielding placed all around the whole part
content.explanation: A wet bench magnetizes by head shot (contacts) and by coil, and circulates a wet particle bath, often with a UV-A lamp for fluorescent inspection.
distractors: A bench offers more than a yoke; it has contacts and a coil.
A bench includes magnetizing hardware, not only a UV lamp.
A bench is not a radiation-shielding device.

content.stem: The head and tailstock on a bench are used to:
options: Clamp the part and pass current for a circular field
Apply developer onto the whole part surface
Demagnetize the finished part and nothing else
Measure the white viewing light level at the surface
content.explanation: The contacts hold the part and pass current through it, producing a circular field (head shot) for longitudinal flaws.
distractors: The contacts magnetize; they do not apply developer.
They are used to magnetize, not only to demagnetize.
They do not measure white light.

content.stem: The coil on a bench provides:
options: A longitudinal field for transverse flaws
A circular field running around the whole part
No magnetic field present at all
Ultraviolet (UV-A) viewing light only
content.explanation: The bench coil magnetizes the part longitudinally, complementing the head shot so both flaw orientations can be covered.
distractors: The coil gives a longitudinal, not circular, field.
The coil does produce a field.
The coil magnetizes; it is not a UV-A light.

content.stem: A portable prod kit magnetizes by:
options: Passing current through the part between two tips
Inducing a field with no contact at all
Spraying magnetic particles onto the part surface only
Emitting ultraviolet (UV-A) light at the part
content.explanation: A prod kit passes current through the part between the tips, creating a local circular field, useful for large weldments and structures.
distractors: Prods make contact and pass current; they are not contactless.
A prod kit magnetizes; spraying particles is a separate step.
Prods magnetize; they do not emit UV-A.

content.stem: A central conductor is:
options: A conductor run through a hollow part for a circular field
A particular type of magnetic particle product used
An ultraviolet (UV-A) viewing lamp unit used inside the booth
A demagnetizing device used after the test only
content.explanation: A central conductor (bar or cable) carries current through the bore of a ring or tube, magnetizing it circularly without current through the part.
distractors: A central conductor is hardware, not a particle.
It is a current-carrying conductor, not a UV lamp.
It magnetizes for inspection, not only demagnetizes.

content.stem: For fluorescent MT, the equipment includes a:
options: A UV-A lamp and a darkened viewing area
A bright white floodlight on its own
The magnetizing yoke used as the light
A radiographic film densitometer unit
content.explanation: Fluorescent particles are read under a UV-A lamp in low ambient light. A UV radiometer verifies the lamp's intensity at the surface.
distractors: A white floodlight would wash out fluorescent indications.
The yoke magnetizes; it is not a light source.
A densitometer is radiographic film equipment.

content.stem: UV-A intensity at the inspection surface is measured with a:
options: A UV radiometer
A white-light meter
A gauss meter
A tape measure
content.explanation: A UV radiometer reads UV-A irradiance to confirm it meets the required minimum (commonly cited near 1000 microwatts per square centimeter at the surface; confirm against the specification).
distractors: A white-light meter reads visible illuminance, not UV-A.
A gauss meter reads magnetic field, not UV-A.
A tape measure reads distance, not UV-A.

content.stem: Visible-particle inspection light level is checked with a:
options: A white-light illuminance meter
A handheld UV radiometer probe
A portable surface hardness tester
A panel-mounted current ammeter
content.explanation: A white-light meter confirms the surface illuminance meets the minimum for visible inspection (commonly cited near 100 foot-candles or about 1000 lux; confirm against the specification).
distractors: A UV radiometer measures UV-A, not white light.
A hardness tester measures hardness.
An ammeter measures current, not light.

content.stem: A pie gauge (magnetic field indicator) is used to:
options: Show the presence and direction of the surface field
Measure the exact magnetic field strength value in gauss
Demagnetize the part that is being tested here
Read the white viewing light level at the surface
content.explanation: A pie gauge shows whether an adequate field is present and its direction at the surface, but it does not give a numeric field strength.
distractors: A pie gauge indicates presence and direction, not an exact magnitude.
A pie gauge is an indicator, not a demagnetizer.
A pie gauge does not read white light.

content.stem: A QQI (quantitative quality indicator) or shim is used to:
options: Verify field direction and adequacy in the area
Apply the magnetic particles onto the part surface
Measure the surface hardness of the part
Provide ultraviolet (UV-A) viewing light
content.explanation: QQIs/shims carry known artificial flaws; placed on the surface, they confirm a field of adequate strength and correct direction is reaching the inspection area.
distractors: QQIs verify the field; they do not apply particles.
QQIs are field indicators, not hardness testers.
QQIs do not provide UV-A light.

content.stem: A gauss/Hall-effect meter reads:
options: The magnetic field strength
Radiographic film density only
White-light surface illuminance
Only the current frequency value
content.explanation: A gauss or Hall-effect meter measures magnetic field strength, useful for checking magnetization and residual fields after demagnetization.
distractors: Film density is a radiographic measurement.
Illuminance is measured by a light meter.
Frequency is not what a gauss meter primarily reads.

content.stem: A Ketos (Betz) test ring is used to:
options: Evaluate system performance using known reference holes
Demagnetize the finished parts after all testing
Hold the part steady throughout the entire inspection run
Measure the white viewing light level at the surface
content.explanation: The reference ring has subsurface holes at known depths; the number of holes shown checks the sensitivity and performance of the particles and equipment together.
distractors: The test ring evaluates performance; it is not a demagnetizer.
It is a reference standard, not a part fixture.
It does not measure white light.

content.stem: A settling (centrifuge) tube is used with wet particles to check:
options: The bath particle concentration
The magnetic field strength value
The UV-A viewing light intensity
The surface hardness of the part
content.explanation: A measured bath sample is settled in a graduated tube; the settled volume indicates particle concentration, which is kept within the procedure range.
distractors: Field strength is checked with field indicators, not a settling tube.
UV-A intensity is read by a radiometer.
Part hardness is unrelated to the settling tube.

content.stem: A wet bench keeps particles in suspension using:
options: A pump and agitation system
An ultraviolet (UV) viewing lamp
A separate demagnetizing coil
A long steel measuring tape
content.explanation: Continuous circulation and agitation keep wet particles evenly suspended so the bath delivers a consistent concentration to the part.
distractors: A UV lamp lights fluorescent particles; it does not suspend them.
A demagnetizer removes residual field; it does not agitate the bath.
A tape measure does not agitate the bath.

content.stem: A demagnetizer (such as an AC demagnetizing coil) is used to:
options: Remove residual magnetism from the part afterward
Magnetize the part and get it ready for inspection
Apply developer onto the part surface
Measure the light level at the surface
content.explanation: Demagnetizing equipment reduces the part's residual field after inspection, commonly by passing it through a decaying AC field.
distractors: Demagnetizers remove field; magnetizing is a separate step.
Demagnetizers do not apply developer.
Demagnetizers do not measure light.

content.stem: Flexible cables and clamps are used to:
options: Wrap coils or make connections for large parts
Take the place of the magnetic particles entirely
Provide ultraviolet (UV-A) viewing light
Demagnetize the part fully automatically
content.explanation: Cables can be wrapped as coils or connected for prod/contact shots on large or awkward parts, extending the equipment's reach.
distractors: Cables carry current; they do not replace particles.
Cables do not provide UV-A light.
Cables are part of magnetizing, not automatic demagnetizing.

content.stem: The ammeter on a magnetizing unit shows:
options: The magnetizing current being applied
The level of the white viewing light used
The UV-A viewing light intensity
The bath particle concentration
content.explanation: The ammeter displays the current, helping the technician set the value the procedure requires. Field indicators still confirm the surface field.
distractors: White light is read by a separate light meter.
UV-A is read by a radiometer.
Particle concentration is checked by a settling tube.

content.stem: A permanent-magnet yoke is sometimes used where:
options: No electrical power is available
Deep subsurface flaws are sought
The part is nonmagnetic metal
Maximum field control is needed
content.explanation: Permanent-magnet yokes need no power, useful in some field or hazardous-area situations, but they offer less field control than electromagnetic yokes and cannot be switched off.
distractors: MT in general does not find deep subsurface flaws.
A yoke cannot magnetize a nonmagnetic part.
Electromagnetic yokes, not permanent magnets, give better field control.

content.stem: Before use, MT equipment should be:
options: Checked for proper function and calibration as needed
Used regardless of its actual working condition at all
Assumed to be always correct without any check
Painted over freshly before each and every use
content.explanation: Functional checks and required calibrations (meters, ammeters, lights, yoke lift) confirm the equipment performs before inspection.
distractors: Faulty equipment can invalidate results.
Equipment is verified, not assumed.
Painting is unrelated to equipment readiness.

content.stem: A UV-A lamp used for fluorescent MT typically requires:
options: Warm-up time and an intensity check at the surface
No checks of any kind at all before using it
Pointing the beam straight into the operator's eyes
Use outdoors in bright direct sunlight
content.explanation: UV-A lamps warm up to stable output and are verified with a radiometer; fluorescent inspection is done in low ambient light, not bright sunlight.
distractors: UV-A output is checked, not ignored.
The lamp must not be pointed at the eyes.
Bright sunlight washes out fluorescent indications.

content.stem: A field indicator should be placed:
options: On the part surface in the area inspected
Deep inside the main power supply unit itself
Inside the connecting cable run
Well away from the part entirely
content.explanation: Field indicators are placed on the surface where flaws are sought, so they confirm the field that the flaws will actually experience.
distractors: The field at the power supply is not the surface field.
Inside the cable is not the inspection area.
Placing it away from the part does not confirm the inspection-area field.

content.stem: A wet fluorescent bench is usually operated:
options: In a darkened area using a UV-A lamp
In bright white overhead room lighting
With no lamp of any kind at all
Outdoors under the midday sun
content.explanation: Fluorescent indications are read under UV-A with low ambient light, so wet fluorescent benches are in darkened areas or hoods.
distractors: Bright white light washes out fluorescent indications.
A UV-A lamp is needed for fluorescent inspection.
Noon sunlight would wash out the indications.

content.stem: Prod tips are commonly made of materials chosen to:
options: Reduce overheating and contact damage while carrying current
Glow brightly under ultraviolet (UV) viewing light
Fully insulate the prod tips so they carry no current at all
Take the place of the magnetic particles entirely
content.explanation: Prod tips must carry current with good contact while limiting heating and burns; some specifications restrict bare copper tips for this reason.
distractors: Prod tips are not designed to fluoresce.
