Prods must carry current, so tips are not full insulators.
Prod tips magnetize; they do not replace particles.

content.stem: Light meters and radiometers used to verify conditions must be:
options: Calibrated and maintained for reliable readings
Used while still completely uncalibrated anyway
Replaced by rough visual estimation
Ignored and simply not used at all
content.explanation: Out-of-calibration meters give untrustworthy readings, so they are calibrated and maintained to confirm UV-A and white-light levels validly.
distractors: Uncalibrated meters cannot be trusted.
Estimating light levels is not acceptable for verification.
Meters are used, not ignored, to verify conditions.

content.stem: When a cable is used as a central conductor through several rings, the technician should:
options: Follow procedure limits on the parts and the current
Use unlimited parts and unlimited current every time
Skip any field check entirely each time
Use it only on nonmagnetic aluminum parts
content.explanation: Field adequacy must be maintained for each part, so the procedure limits the arrangement and sets the current; field indicators confirm the field reaches each part.
distractors: There are limits on the number of parts and the current for adequate field.
Field checks confirm adequacy and are not skipped.
Central conductors are used on ferromagnetic parts, not aluminum.

content.stem: For field inspection of a weld with no shop power nearby, a practical choice is:
options: A portable yoke, AC, DC, or permanent magnet
A large stationary wet horizontal bench unit
A full central-conductor bench setup
A radiographic film processor unit
content.explanation: A portable yoke suits field weld inspection. Stationary benches and bench central-conductor setups are shop equipment; a film processor belongs to radiography.
distractors: A stationary wet bench is not portable field equipment.
A bench central-conductor setup is shop equipment.
A film processor is for radiography, not MT.

content.stem: With equipment, the Level I technician is generally expected to:
options: Operate it and run routine functional checks under direction
Design brand-new inspection equipment completely from scratch
Approve the equipment calibration intervals himself
Certify the whole inspection system on his own
content.explanation: A Level I operates the equipment and performs routine checks, recording results, while higher levels handle calibration intervals and qualification.
distractors: Designing equipment is not a Level I function.
Setting calibration intervals is above the Level I.
Independent system certification is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: Reference standards like the Ketos ring and QQIs exist to:
options: Confirm the system and field perform as expected
Take the place of the actual test part
Demagnetize the parts after all testing
Measure the outside dimensions of the whole part
content.explanation: These standards verify that particles, current, and field are performing, giving confidence the inspection can reveal real flaws.
distractors: They are checks, not substitutes for the actual part.
They are performance standards, not demagnetizers.
They do not measure part dimensions.

content.stem: Which statement about MT equipment is correct?
options: Several devices magnetize, while meters and indicators verify conditions
All magnetic particle testing is always done using only a single yoke
Field indicators are the devices that actually apply the magnetic particles
UV radiometers are the meters used to measure the magnetizing current
content.explanation: Different equipment magnetizes in different ways, and meters, field indicators, and reference standards verify the field, lighting, and system performance. A yoke is one option among several.
distractors: MT uses several magnetizing devices, not only a yoke.
Field indicators verify the field; they do not apply particles.
UV radiometers measure UV-A light, not current.

content.stem: Magnetic particles are supplied as:
options: Dry powders or wet liquid suspensions
Only as dry powders and never wet
Only as gases sprayed onto the surface
Only as fused-on solid coatings
content.explanation: Particles come as dry powder or suspended in a liquid carrier (wet). Each form suits different surfaces and flaw types.
distractors: Wet suspensions are also available, not only dry.
Particles are not used as gases.
Particles are applied loosely, not fused to the part.

content.stem: Magnetic particles can be visible or fluorescent, where fluorescent particles are read under:
options: Ultraviolet (UV-A) light
Bright white visible light
No light source at all
Plain infrared light
content.explanation: Fluorescent particles glow under UV-A in low ambient light for high sensitivity; visible particles are read under white light by color contrast.
distractors: Bright white light is for visible particles, not fluorescent.
Fluorescent particles need UV-A to glow.
Fluorescent particles respond to UV-A, not infrared.

content.stem: Visible particle color is chosen to:
options: Contrast with the surface being inspected
Match the part surface color almost exactly
Glow brightly under the UV light
Be completely invisible to the eye
content.explanation: Visible particles come in colors such as gray, black, red, and yellow so the technician can pick a color that stands out against the part.
distractors: Matching the surface would hide indications.
Glowing under UV describes fluorescent particles.
Particles are made to be seen, not invisible.

content.stem: Dry particles are generally preferred for:
options: Rough surfaces, subsurface flaws, and field work
Fine surface cracks on smooth, well-polished parts
Nonmagnetic parts like aluminum and brass
Underwater inspection work only
content.explanation: Dry powder suits rough or hot surfaces, gives good subsurface sensitivity (especially with HWDC), and is convenient in the field.
distractors: Fine surface cracks on smooth parts are better served by the wet method.
Dry particles still need a ferromagnetic part.
Dry powder is not specifically an underwater method.

content.stem: Wet particles are generally preferred for:
options: Fine surface cracks on relatively smooth parts
Very rough cast iron castings only
Nonmagnetic parts like aluminum, brass, and copper
Dry, very hot part surfaces only
content.explanation: Wet suspensions, especially fluorescent, give high sensitivity to fine surface cracks and are common on machined and smoother parts.
distractors: Very rough castings are often better suited to the dry method.
Wet particles still require a ferromagnetic part.
Wet suspensions are not applied to dry hot surfaces.

content.stem: The highest sensitivity to fine surface cracks is usually given by:
options: Wet fluorescent particles viewed under UV-A
Dry visible powder seen in white light
No particles applied to the part at all
Visible red particles on a red painted surface
content.explanation: Wet fluorescent particles read under UV-A in a darkened area provide the greatest sensitivity to small surface flaws.
distractors: Dry visible powder is less sensitive to fine surface cracks than wet fluorescent.
Particles are required to form indications.
Red particles on a red surface give no contrast.

content.stem: Dry powder should be applied as:
options: A light, even cloud drifting onto the surface
A heavy pile dumped on all at once
A liquid spray applied directly onto the part surface
A flood of solvent poured over it
content.explanation: Dry particles are dusted on gently as a light cloud so they can move to leakage fields. A heavy pile masks indications.
distractors: A dumped pile buries indications and does not let particles move.
Dry powder is applied dry, not as a liquid spray.
A solvent flood is not how dry powder is applied.

content.stem: Excess dry powder is removed by:
options: A gentle air stream leaving particles at the flaws
A full rinse of water poured over the entire part
Wiping it down hard with a cloth rag
Adding even more dry powder right on top
content.explanation: A light air current blows off loose excess while particles held by leakage fields remain, revealing the indication.
distractors: Dry powder is not rinsed with water during inspection.
Hard wiping would remove the indication too.
Adding more powder increases background rather than clearing excess.

content.stem: Wet particles are applied by:
options: Flowing, spraying, or immersing to cover the whole area
Dusting it on lightly as a dry floating powder cloud overhead
Blowing it onto the part with a stream of air
Wiping it onto the surface with a dry cloth rag
content.explanation: The wet bath is gently flowed or sprayed over the part, or the part is immersed, so suspended particles can migrate to flaws.
distractors: Dusting a dry cloud is the dry method.
Air blowing is for removing dry excess, not applying wet bath.
A dry rag does not apply a wet suspension.

content.stem: Good magnetic particles have:
options: High permeability, so they respond to leakage fields
Low permeability and only a weak field response
High retentivity, so they tend to clump together badly
No magnetic response to the leakage field at all
content.explanation: Particles should magnetize easily (high permeability) to be drawn to leakage fields, and have low retentivity so they do not clump or stay magnetized.
distractors: Low permeability would make particles respond poorly.
High retentivity would cause clumping and is undesirable.
Particles must respond magnetically to work.

content.stem: Magnetic particles are made with low retentivity so that they:
options: Do not stay magnetized and clump together
Hold on to a permanent magnetic field forever
Glow more brightly under the UV light
Dissolve readily in plain water
content.explanation: Low retentivity keeps particles from becoming little magnets that stick together, which would reduce mobility and cause false buildup.
distractors: A permanent field on particles would cause clumping.
Retentivity does not control glow; fluorescent dye does.
Retentivity is unrelated to dissolving.

content.stem: Magnetic particle products often blend elongated and rounded particles to balance:
options: Strong indication formation with good mobility
Particle color against the overall particle weight
Material cost against the packaging size
Use under UV against use in white light
content.explanation: Elongated particles align well in leakage fields to build strong indications, while rounded particles add mobility, so a mix is used.
distractors: The blend is about magnetic behavior, not color and weight.
The blend is for performance, not packaging.
Particle shape is unrelated to which light is used.

content.stem: Wet bath particle concentration is kept within limits because:
options: Too high raises background; too low weakens indications
It changes the UV viewing light wavelength used
It sets the magnetizing current level
It controls the overall surface hardness of the whole part
content.explanation: Excess particles cause heavy background; too few give faint indications. Concentration is checked with a settling tube and kept in range.
distractors: Concentration does not change UV wavelength.
Concentration does not set the magnetizing current.
Concentration is unrelated to part hardness.

content.stem: Bath concentration is verified using a:
options: A settling tube reading the settled particle volume
A gauss meter used for reading the magnetic field strength
A UV radiometer for reading UV-A
A pie gauge used for checking the field direction
content.explanation: A measured sample settles in a graduated tube; the settled volume indicates concentration, compared against the procedure range.
distractors: A gauss meter reads field strength, not concentration.
A UV radiometer reads UV-A intensity.
A pie gauge indicates field direction, not concentration.

content.stem: Wet particle carriers are typically:
options: Water-based or light oil-based liquids
Always strong acidic chemical solutions
Always solvents such as acetone alone
Always hot molten liquid metal
content.explanation: Wet suspensions use a water carrier (with conditioners) or a light petroleum distillate. Acids, harsh solvents, and molten metal are not carriers.
distractors: Strong acids are not used as particle carriers.
Aggressive solvents like acetone are not standard carriers.
Molten metal is not a particle carrier.

content.stem: Water-based carriers include conditioners (wetting agents) to:
options: Help the bath wet evenly and resist corrosion and foaming
Make the part nonmagnetic during the whole test
Increase the magnetic retentivity of all the particles used
Provide ultraviolet light for viewing the part
content.explanation: Conditioners promote even wetting, control foaming, and add corrosion inhibition so the water bath performs and does not harm parts.
distractors: Conditioners do not make the part nonmagnetic.
Conditioners are not added to raise retentivity.
Conditioners do not provide UV light.

content.stem: A water-break test on a water-bath part checks that the surface:
options: Is clean enough for the bath to wet it evenly
Has already been properly magnetized
Is at exactly the right surface hardness value
Has exactly the correct surface color
content.explanation: If water sheets evenly without breaking into beads, the surface is clean enough for uniform bath coverage; beading indicates contamination.
distractors: The water-break test checks wetting/cleanliness, not magnetization.
It does not check hardness.
It does not check color.

content.stem: A wet bath should be checked for contamination such as:
options: Dirt, oil, wrong-carrier water, or particle breakdown
The correct part number for the whole job order
The magnetic field strength that is present here
The white viewing light level right at the part surface
content.explanation: Contaminants and degraded particles reduce performance, so the bath is monitored and replaced when out of limits.
distractors: Part numbers are a parts matter, not a bath contamination check.
Field strength is checked with field indicators, not the bath.
White light level is a viewing condition, not a bath property.

content.stem: In the continuous wet method, the bath is applied and then:
options: Flow is stopped just before or as the current is applied
Current is never used at any point at all
The part is then fully demagnetized
The bath is left flowing the whole time the current is on
content.explanation: Particles are applied, then bath flow is stopped as the magnetizing current is applied so particles are not washed away while indications form. Exact timing follows the procedure.
distractors: Current is essential to form indications in the continuous method.
Demagnetizing comes after inspection, not during application.
Heavy flow during the current can wash particles off forming indications.

content.stem: With dry powder in the continuous method, powder is applied:
options: While the field is present, then the excess is blown off
Only after the magnetizing field has been fully switched off
With no magnetic field present in the part at all
Mixed into a liquid carrier beforehand first
content.explanation: Dry powder is dusted on while the field is applied so particles gather at flaws, then loose excess is gently removed. Dry powder is not mixed into liquid.
distractors: Applying only after the field is off is the residual approach, less sensitive.
A field is needed to form indications.
Dry powder is used dry, not mixed into liquid.

content.stem: On a dark steel surface, a good visible particle color choice is:
options: A light color such as gray or yellow for contrast
Black particles used just for the surface contrast
A color that closely matches the steel part
An invisible particle coating layer on top
content.explanation: A light particle color contrasts with dark steel. Black would blend in, and matching colors hide indications.
distractors: Black particles blend into dark steel.
Matching the steel hides indications.
Particles must be visible, not invisible.

content.stem: Fluorescent particles require which viewing condition?
options: Low ambient white light plus UV-A
Bright white overhead room light
No UV source present at all
Direct outdoor midday sunlight
content.explanation: Fluorescent indications are read under UV-A with low ambient white light so the glow stands out. Bright light or sunlight washes them out.
distractors: Bright white light washes out fluorescent indications.
A UV-A source is required for fluorescence.
Direct sunlight washes out fluorescent indications.

content.stem: Dry particles can be used on warm parts where wet baths might:
options: Boil off or become unsafe
Actually perform much better
Be the only required choice
Glow under the UV lamp
content.explanation: On hot surfaces, a water or oil bath may flash off or create hazards, so dry powder rated for the temperature is used instead.
distractors: Wet baths can perform poorly or unsafely on hot parts.
Wet baths are not required on hot parts; dry is often used.
Dry particles do not glow unless they are fluorescent-coated for UV use.

content.stem: Oil-based wet carriers are a consideration because they:
options: Can be flammable and need safety controls
Are radioactive sources of their own
Are always completely nonflammable liquids
Magnetize the part all by themselves
content.explanation: Petroleum-distillate carriers can be flammable, so flash point, ventilation, and ignition control matter. They do not magnetize the part themselves.
distractors: Oil carriers are not radioactive.
Many oil carriers are flammable, not always nonflammable.
The carrier suspends particles; the current magnetizes the part.

content.stem: If wet bath concentration is too high, the likely result is:
options: Heavy background that masks real indications
Faint, weak indications showing on the part surface
No indications forming on the part at all
Better detection of fine surface cracks
content.explanation: Excess particles settle over the whole surface, raising background and hiding genuine indications, so concentration is reduced into range.
distractors: Faint indications result from too low, not too high, concentration.
Indications can still form, but background masks them.
Excess concentration hurts, not helps, fine-crack detection.

content.stem: If wet bath concentration is too low, the likely result is:
options: Weak or missing indications
Heavy, masking background
Furring across the whole part
Better overall sensitivity
content.explanation: Too few particles cannot build a clear indication, so real flaws may be missed. Concentration is raised into range.
distractors: Heavy background comes from too high a concentration.
Furring is associated with excess field or particles, not a low bath.
Low concentration lowers, not raises, sensitivity.

content.stem: Very fine particles are good for fine flaws but can:
options: Cause more background if not controlled
Never form any indications at all
Work only in the dry powder method
Magnetize the whole part all by themselves
content.explanation: Fine particles are sensitive to small flaws yet can adhere more readily as background, so concentration and process are controlled. They do not magnetize the part.
distractors: Fine particles do form indications.
Fine particles are used in both wet and dry systems.
Particles respond to the part's field; they do not magnetize it.

content.stem: Aerosol cans of wet particles are convenient for:
options: Portable field and spot inspection
Large immersion-bath bench processing
Replacing the magnetizing source itself
Demagnetizing the finished part
content.explanation: Aerosol wet particles (visible or fluorescent) suit portable and field work alongside a yoke or prods. They do not magnetize or demagnetize.
distractors: Large immersion processing uses bench bath systems, not aerosols.
Aerosol particles do not magnetize the part.
Aerosol particles do not demagnetize the part.

content.stem: Particles must be present at the surface:
options: While the leakage field exists, so they gather at flaws
Only after the part has completely cooled down
Only after the whole part has first been fully demagnetized
With no magnetic field present anywhere at all
content.explanation: Indications form when particles are at the surface during the magnetizing field. In the residual method the field is the retained one, but a field must still be present.
distractors: Cooling is not the trigger; the field presence is.
Demagnetizing removes the field needed to form indications.
A field, applied or residual, must be present to form indications.

content.stem: Particle mobility is important because particles must:
options: Move freely to reach and gather at leakage fields
Stay completely fixed in one single place on the part
Dissolve into the metal body of the part
Evaporate off the part surface entirely
content.explanation: Particles need to migrate to leakage fields to build indications, which is why mobility (from low retentivity, carrier flow, or air) matters.
distractors: Fixed particles cannot gather at flaws.
Particles sit on the surface; they do not dissolve in.
Particles accumulate at flaws; they do not evaporate.

content.stem: For fluorescent wet inspection, the bath and part should be free of:
options: Stray fluorescing contamination that gives false background
All the magnetic particles, leaving absolutely none behind at all
The applied magnetizing field itself entirely
Any of the liquid carrier fluid in the bath
content.explanation: Contaminants that fluoresce raise background and cause confusion, so cleanliness is maintained for fluorescent work.
distractors: Particles are needed; the bath is not meant to be particle-free.
A field is required to form indications.
The carrier liquid is part of the wet method.

content.stem: Selecting dry versus wet particles depends mainly on:
options: Surface, flaw type, sensitivity, and the conditions
The mood of the inspector on that day
Only the painted outer color of the part
The particular time of the working day it happens to be done
content.explanation: Rough or hot surfaces and subsurface flaws favor dry; fine surface cracks on smoother parts favor wet. Sensitivity needs and field conditions also matter.
distractors: Mood does not determine the particle choice.
Part color alone does not drive dry versus wet.
Time of day is irrelevant.

content.stem: Magnetic particle materials should be:
options: Stored and used within spec and kept uncontaminated
Used well past their printed expiry date anyway
Mixed together randomly across several different products
Left exposed to dirt and grime while in storage
content.explanation: Materials are kept within shelf life and protected from contamination so they perform as qualified. Mixing products is not done without qualification.
distractors: Expired materials may underperform.
Random mixing of products can degrade performance.
Dirt contamination degrades the materials.

content.stem: Fluorescent particles are chosen over visible mainly for:
options: Higher sensitivity to small flaws
Working in bright open daylight
Avoiding the need for any UV-A
Use on nonmagnetic aluminum parts
content.explanation: Fluorescent systems detect smaller flaws but require UV-A and a darkened area. Visible systems are simpler where high sensitivity is not needed.
distractors: Fluorescent inspection needs low ambient light, not bright daylight.
Fluorescent particles require a UV-A source.
Particle type does not change the need for a ferromagnetic part.

content.stem: Wet bath concentration and condition are checked:
options: At intervals set by the procedure
Only once, when it is first mixed
Never checked at any point at all
Only after a part has been rejected
content.explanation: Concentration and contamination are verified on a schedule so the bath stays in range, catching drift before it affects results.
distractors: A one-time check does not catch later drift.
Bath checks are required, not skipped.
Checks are scheduled to prevent problems, not only done after rejections.

content.stem: Which statement about particles and media is correct?
options: Dry suits rough, subsurface, field work; wet suits fine cracks
Wet particles are always the very best choice for every single job
Particle color makes no real difference at all
Bath concentration has no real effect on results
content.explanation: Dry and wet each have their place, fluorescent gives the highest sensitivity, and color contrast and bath concentration are controlled for valid results.
distractors: Wet is not always best; dry suits rough, hot, and subsurface work.
Color contrast matters for visible particles.
Bath concentration strongly affects results.

content.stem: A typical MT sequence is:
options: Clean, magnetize, apply particles, inspect, record, then demagnetize
Develop, expose, and then interpret the finished radiographic film image
Heat, quench, and then temper the steel part during heat treatment
Etch the part surface chemically and do nothing else at all
content.explanation: The process prepares the surface, magnetizes, applies particles and inspects, records, then demagnetizes and cleans as required.
distractors: Develop, expose, interpret describes radiography.
Heat, quench, temper are heat-treatment steps.
Etching alone is a surface-prep step, not the MT sequence.

content.stem: Pre-cleaning before MT is done to:
options: Remove dirt, scale, or coatings that hide indications
Magnetize the whole part ready for the test
Apply the magnetic particles onto the whole part surface
Demagnetize the whole part well beforehand first
content.explanation: Contaminants impede particle movement and can mask indications, so the surface is cleaned appropriately before magnetizing.
distractors: Cleaning does not magnetize the part.
Cleaning precedes particle application; it is not the same step.
Cleaning is not demagnetizing.

content.stem: In the continuous method, particles are applied:
options: While the magnetizing field is present
After the magnetizing field has been removed
Before any cleaning is done at all
Only during the final demagnetizing step
content.explanation: The continuous method applies particles while the field is on, giving maximum sensitivity because the leakage field is present as indications form.
distractors: Applying after the field is removed is the residual method.
Cleaning comes before particle application.
Particles are applied during magnetizing, not demagnetizing.

content.stem: In the residual method, particles are applied:
options: After the force is removed, using the retained field
While the magnetizing current is still flowing through it
Before the part has been cleaned at all
Only when a magnetic yoke is being used
content.explanation: The residual method relies on the part's retained field after magnetizing, so it only works on materials with sufficient retentivity.
distractors: Applying while current flows is the continuous method.
Cleaning precedes particle application.
The residual method is defined by timing, not by using a yoke.

content.stem: Compared with the residual method, the continuous method is generally:
options: More sensitive overall
Less sensitive overall
Only for nonmagnetic parts
Never actually used
content.explanation: Because the field is present as particles gather, the continuous method gives stronger indications and higher sensitivity, and is the more common choice.
distractors: The continuous method is more, not less, sensitive.
Neither method works on nonmagnetic parts.
The continuous method is widely used.

content.stem: The residual method is suitable only when the part:
options: Has enough retentivity to hold an adequate field
Is made of a fully nonmagnetic material
Has been painted over completely well beforehand
Cannot be cleaned properly at all anywhere
content.explanation: Only materials that retain a strong field after magnetizing can support the residual method; low-retentivity materials require the continuous method.
distractors: Nonmagnetic parts cannot be inspected by MT at all.
Paint would need removal; it does not enable the residual method.
Cleaning is still required; cleanability is not the deciding factor.

content.stem: A complete MT of a part usually includes:
options: Magnetizing and inspecting in two perpendicular directions
Inspecting in only one single fixed field direction throughout
Skipping the inspection step entirely each time
Doing only the demagnetization step at the end
content.explanation: To cover flaws of all orientations, the part is magnetized and inspected in at least two perpendicular directions (or multidirectionally).
distractors: One direction misses flaws aligned with that field.
Inspection is essential to the process.
Demagnetization alone does not inspect the part.

content.stem: In wet continuous inspection, bath flow is stopped:
options: As or just before the magnetizing current is applied
Long after the magnetizing current has completely ended
Never stopped at any point at all
Only during the final demagnetizing step
content.explanation: Stopping bath flow as the current is applied prevents particles from being washed off the forming indications, per the procedure's timing.
distractors: Leaving heavy flow during the current can wash away indications.
Flow is controlled relative to the current, not left running.
Bath timing relates to magnetizing, not demagnetizing.

content.stem: In dry continuous inspection, the correct order is:
options: Apply the field, dust on powder, remove excess, observe
Dust on the powder and never magnetize the part at all anyway
Demagnetize first, then dust on the powder
Apply penetrant first, then dust on powder
content.explanation: With the field applied, powder is dusted on, loose excess is gently removed, and indications are observed while the field is present.
distractors: A field must be applied for indications to form.
Demagnetizing first removes the field needed to form indications.
Penetrant belongs to PT, not the MT dry sequence.

content.stem: When inspecting a large area in sections, the technician should:
options: Overlap sections so no area lacks field or particles
Leave wide gaps between the sections just to save time
Inspect just a single small spot on it
Skip the edges of the inspection area
content.explanation: Overlapping ensures full coverage with an adequate field and particle application everywhere, leaving no strip uninspected.
distractors: Gaps risk missing flaws between sections.
One spot is not full coverage.
Edges must be included in the coverage.

content.stem: In the continuous method, indications are best observed:
options: While the field and particles are present, or just after
Days and days later, long after the whole test is finished
After the part has been fully post-cleaned afterward
After the whole part has been demagnetized
content.explanation: Indications are viewed while the field holds the particles, since removing the field or cleaning would disturb them.
distractors: Waiting days is not how continuous indications are read.
Post-cleaning removes particles and indications.
Demagnetizing removes the field and can disturb indications.

content.stem: In the sequence, cleaning comes:
options: Before magnetizing and applying particles
After the whole inspection is fully finished
After the part has been demagnetized
In between recording and demagnetizing
content.explanation: Surface preparation is first so particles can move and indications can show. It precedes magnetizing, particle application, and inspection.
distractors: Cleaning precedes, not follows, inspection.
Cleaning is before, not after, demagnetizing.
Cleaning is the first step, not inserted late in the sequence.

content.stem: Indications should be recorded:
options: Before the part is demagnetized and cleaned
After post-cleaning has fully removed all of them
Not recorded at any point at all
After the part has already shipped out
content.explanation: Indications are documented while present, before demagnetization and cleaning remove the particle buildup.
distractors: Post-cleaning removes the indication, so recording must come first.
Indications are part of the record.
Recording after shipping is too late.

content.stem: Post-cleaning after MT is done to:
options: Remove particles and any bath residue from the part
Magnetize the whole part again for the test
Form fresh new indications on the whole part surface
Add a thick protective coating onto it
content.explanation: After inspection, particles and carrier residue are removed so the part is left clean for service or further processing.
distractors: Post-cleaning does not magnetize the part.
Indications are formed during inspection, not post-cleaning.
Post-cleaning removes residue rather than adding a coating.

content.stem: Demagnetization, when required, is generally performed:
options: After inspection and recording
Before magnetizing the whole part
Before cleaning the whole part
In place of inspecting it at all
content.explanation: The part is inspected and indications recorded first, then demagnetized if a residual field would cause problems later.
distractors: Demagnetizing before magnetizing makes no sense in the sequence.
Cleaning precedes magnetizing; demagnetizing comes after inspection.
Demagnetization does not replace inspection.

content.stem: The residual method can be convenient because:
options: Particles go on after magnetizing, easing handling on suitable parts
It works on essentially any kind of material there is, anywhere
It needs no magnetic field at all in order to form indications
It is always the more sensitive of the two methods by far overall
content.explanation: Applying particles after the magnetizing step can simplify part handling, but only high-retentivity materials hold an adequate residual field, and sensitivity is generally lower than continuous.
distractors: It works only on high-retentivity materials, not any material.
A residual field must be present from prior magnetizing.
The continuous method is generally more sensitive.

content.stem: The cleaned and inspected area should cover:
options: The required inspection area plus a margin
Only a small single spot on the whole part
The entire shop floor area as well
Nowhere near the actual flaws at all
content.explanation: Cleaning and inspection cover the area of interest with a margin so contaminants and uninspected strips do not compromise results.
distractors: A small spot may leave flaws uninspected.
The shop is not the inspection area.
The flaw areas must be cleaned and inspected.

content.stem: If a part must be reinspected, it should first be:
options: Cleaned of old particles and reprocessed from the right step
Inspected right over the old leftover particles all over again
Left exactly as it is, completely untouched
Painted over completely before any reinspection
content.explanation: Old particle buildup is removed so it does not confuse the new inspection, and the process is repeated as required.
distractors: Old particles can confuse a fresh inspection.
Leaving prior buildup compromises the new test.
Painting would mask the surface and is not done.

content.stem: Most MT is performed using the continuous method because it:
options: Provides higher sensitivity for most parts
Works without any magnetic field being present
Avoids the need for any cleaning
Needs no particles to be applied at all
content.explanation: The continuous method's presence of the field during particle application gives better sensitivity, making it the usual choice.
distractors: A field is required for the continuous method.
Cleaning is still required.
Particles are still required.

content.stem: Recording results is part of the sequence because:
options: It documents the indications and process for traceability
It magnetizes the whole part again for the test
It cleans the whole part completely after the testing is done
It is optional and can simply be skipped each time
content.explanation: Documentation captures what was found and how the test was done, supporting traceability and any later evaluation.
distractors: Recording does not magnetize the part.
Recording does not clean the part.
Recording is required, not skipped.

content.stem: For each magnetizing shot in the sequence, the technician confirms:
options: An adequate field of the intended direction is present
Only that the white viewing light happens to be switched on
The painted outer color of the part
The humidity level in the whole room
content.explanation: Field indicators confirm the right field direction and adequacy for each shot, ensuring the intended flaw orientations are covered.
distractors: Light being on does not confirm the magnetic field.
Part color does not confirm the field.
Humidity does not confirm the field.

content.stem: Application and current timing in the continuous method are:
options: Controlled per procedure for consistent results
Left completely random from one part to the next
Irrelevant to the whole inspection
Set only by the weight of the part
content.explanation: The procedure specifies how particles and current are timed so results are consistent and repeatable across parts.
distractors: Random timing yields inconsistent results.
Timing affects sensitivity and is not irrelevant.
Part weight does not set the timing.

content.stem: After dusting dry powder with the field on, the technician observes for indications:
options: As excess is gently removed and particles stay at flaws
Only after washing it all off with plain water
Only after the whole part has first been fully demagnetized
With no magnetic field present at all
content.explanation: With the field present, gentle removal of loose powder reveals particles held at flaws, which the technician observes and records.
distractors: Dry powder is not washed off with water during inspection.
Demagnetizing removes the field that holds the indication.
A field, applied or residual, must be present.

content.stem: The cleaning and post-cleaning methods used are:
options: Specified by the procedure for the part and situation
Chosen completely at random for each and every separate part
Never needed at any point at all
Based on the painted color of the part
content.explanation: The procedure defines acceptable cleaning and post-cleaning so the process is valid and the part is left in proper condition.
distractors: Cleaning methods are specified, not random.
Cleaning is needed for a valid test and an acceptable finished part.
Part color does not set the cleaning method.

content.stem: Safety practices apply:
options: Throughout the whole sequence, including magnetizing and cleaning
Only at the very end of the whole job, once it has finished
Only during the recording step and at no other point at all
At no point at all during the whole job of work being done
content.explanation: Electrical, chemical, and lighting safety considerations apply across the whole process, not just at one point.
distractors: Safety is not limited to the end of the process.
Safety is not limited to the recording step.
Safety always applies.

content.stem: A thick paint or coating is removed before MT because it:
options: Holds particles off the surface and can mask flaws
Improves the overall inspection sensitivity quite a lot
Is required in order to magnetize the part
Glows on its own under the UV light
content.explanation: A coating separates particles from the surface and can hide indications, so it is removed unless a procedure qualifies inspection through a known thin coating.
distractors: A coating reduces, not improves, sensitivity.
Coatings are not required for magnetizing.
Ordinary coatings are not fluorescent indicators.

content.stem: Through the sequence, the Level I technician:
options: Performs the steps and records results under direction
Sets the formal acceptance criteria for the whole part
Approves the written inspection procedure
Qualifies the whole inspection technique
content.explanation: A Level I carries out the cleaning, magnetizing, particle application, inspection, recording, demagnetizing, and cleaning steps to the procedure, under higher-level direction.
distractors: Acceptance criteria are set above the Level I.
Approving procedures is a Level III function.
Qualifying techniques is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: Which statement about the MT process is correct?
options: Clean, magnetize two ways, apply particles, inspect, record, demagnetize
Inspect the whole part first, well before ever cleaning it at all
Use only one single magnetizing direction the whole time through
Skip the recording of the inspection results entirely each time
content.explanation: The sequence cleans first, magnetizes and inspects in two directions, records, then demagnetizes and post-cleans. The continuous method is the usual, more sensitive choice.
distractors: Cleaning comes before inspection.
Two directions are needed to cover all flaw orientations.
Recording is a required step.

content.stem: Visible (color-contrast) MT is read under white light meeting a specified minimum, commonly cited as:
options: About 100 foot-candles (roughly 1000 lux) at the surface
Complete and total darkness across the whole part surface
UV-A light only present at the surface
Only about 1 single foot-candle at the part surface
content.explanation: Visible particle inspection needs adequate white light at the surface, commonly around 100 foot-candles (about 1000 lux). Confirm the exact value against the governing specification.
distractors: Visible inspection needs light, not darkness.
UV-A is for fluorescent particles, not visible.
About 1 foot-candle is far too dim for visible inspection.

content.stem: Fluorescent MT requires a UV-A irradiance at the surface commonly cited as at least:
options: About 1000 microwatts per square centimeter
Effectively zero right at the whole part surface
About 100 foot-candles of white light
Only 1 microwatt per square centimeter
content.explanation: Fluorescent inspection commonly requires UV-A of at least roughly 1000 microwatts per square centimeter at the surface. Confirm the exact value against the governing specification.
distractors: Some UV-A is required; zero would not excite the particles.
100 foot-candles describes white light, not UV-A.
1 microwatt per square centimeter is far too low.

content.stem: For fluorescent inspection, ambient white light is kept:
options: Low, such as a couple of foot-candles maximum
As bright as it can possibly be made, fully on
At about a full 100 foot-candles
Irrelevant to the whole inspection
content.explanation: Low ambient white light lets fluorescent indications stand out. Specifications set a maximum (often only a couple of foot-candles); confirm the value against the specification.
distractors: Bright ambient light washes out fluorescent indications.
100 foot-candles is a visible-light level, too bright for fluorescent viewing.
Ambient light level matters for fluorescent inspection.

content.stem: Before fluorescent inspection, the technician's eyes should:
options: Be allowed to adapt to the low light for a short time
Stare directly into the bright UV lamp for a while first
Be exposed to bright white light first
Need no adjustment of any kind at all
content.explanation: Eyes need time to adapt to the dark viewing area so faint indications are seen. Specifications set a minimum adaptation time; confirm against the specification.
distractors: Staring at the UV lamp is unsafe and does not aid adaptation.
Bright light just before viewing defeats dark adaptation.
Some adaptation time is needed for reliable viewing.

content.stem: When using a UV-A lamp, the technician should:
options: Avoid looking into the beam and wear proper eyewear
Look straight into the beam directly just to check it
Remove all of the eyewear while viewing
Aim it toward any nearby coworkers
content.explanation: UV-A should not be viewed directly; suitable UV-blocking eyewear is used, and the beam is not aimed at people, to protect the eyes and skin.
distractors: Looking into the beam is a hazard, not a check method.
Appropriate eyewear is protective and should be worn.
Aiming UV-A at coworkers exposes them to a hazard.

content.stem: UV-blocking eyewear during fluorescent inspection helps:
options: Protect the eyes and improve indication contrast
Magnetize the whole part that is being tested here
Increase the UV-A lamp's light output
Take the place of the UV radiometer
content.explanation: UV-blocking lenses protect the eyes and can improve the visibility of fluorescent indications by reducing scattered UV reaching the eye.
distractors: Eyewear does not magnetize the part.
Eyewear does not increase lamp output.
Eyewear does not measure UV-A; a radiometer does.

content.stem: Light meters and UV radiometers used to verify conditions must be:
options: Calibrated and in good condition
Used while still uncalibrated
Replaced by rough guessing instead
Used only one single time, ever
content.explanation: Reliable light verification depends on calibrated, maintained meters; otherwise the readings cannot be trusted.
distractors: Uncalibrated meters give untrustworthy readings.
Guessing is not a valid substitute for measurement.
Meters are used regularly, not only once.

content.stem: Light levels are measured:
options: At the surface in the area inspected
Up high at the ceiling of the room
Deep inside the UV lamp housing
Anywhere that happens to be convenient
content.explanation: Both UV-A and white light are measured at the inspection surface, since that is where the indications must be seen.
distractors: The ceiling is not the inspection surface.
Inside the lamp is not the inspection point.
Measurement must be at the surface, not just any spot.

content.stem: A linear indication (length much greater than width) commonly suggests:
options: A crack, seam, or lap
Rounded gas porosity
A perfectly clean surface
A fault in the light meter
content.explanation: Linear indications typically come from crack-like flaws such as cracks, seams, and laps. Evaluation against criteria is a higher-level step.
distractors: Rounded porosity gives rounded, not linear, indications.
A clean surface gives no indication.
An indication is a particle pattern, not a meter fault.

content.stem: A rounded indication commonly suggests:
options: A gas pore or similar rounded condition
A long, thin crack in the part
A keyway placed there on purpose by design
No discontinuity present there at all
content.explanation: Rounded indications often arise from porosity or similar rounded conditions. Their significance is judged during evaluation.
distractors: A long crack gives a linear indication.
A keyway is a geometric feature giving a nonrelevant indication, not a rounded flaw.
A rounded indication does reflect a condition to be assessed.

content.stem: A relevant (true) indication is one that:
options: Is caused by an actual discontinuity
Comes from the part's own geometry
Comes from surface contamination only
Is always rejectable right on sight
content.explanation: Relevant indications arise from real discontinuities. Whether they are acceptable depends on evaluation against the criteria, a higher-level task.
distractors: Indications from geometry are nonrelevant, not relevant flaws.
Indications from contamination are false, not relevant.
Relevance does not by itself mean rejectable; that needs evaluation.

content.stem: A false indication is one that:
options: Comes from contamination, not a flaw or part geometry
Is caused by a real crack found deep inside the part body
Comes from a keyway cut in the part
Is always a forging seam in the part
content.explanation: False indications come from process or handling causes such as dirt, loose scale, or magnetic writing, not from a discontinuity or the part's design.
distractors: An indication from a real crack is relevant, not false.
A keyway gives a nonrelevant (geometry) indication, not a false one.
A seam is a real discontinuity, giving a relevant indication.

content.stem: A nonrelevant indication is one that:
options: Comes from part geometry or design, not a flaw
Comes from a real crack found deep inside the part
Comes from a forging lap in the part
Is always rejectable right on sight
content.explanation: Nonrelevant indications result from design features such as threads, keyways, splines, or abrupt section changes. They are real magnetic effects but not flaws.
distractors: A crack gives a relevant indication.
A lap gives a relevant indication.
Nonrelevant indications are not flaws and are not rejectable.

content.stem: Which commonly produces nonrelevant indications?
options: Threads, keyways, and abrupt section changes
Fatigue cracks formed while in active service
Forging laps formed in the steel part
Quench cracks from rapid part cooling
content.explanation: Geometry features such as threads, keyways, and sharp section changes concentrate flux and can hold particles without any flaw being present.
distractors: Fatigue cracks are real flaws giving relevant indications.
Forging laps are real flaws giving relevant indications.
Quench cracks are real flaws giving relevant indications.

content.stem: Magnetic writing is a false indication caused by:
options: Contact between a magnetized part and another object
A true, real crack found in the part
Correct and full demagnetization of the whole part itself
Adequate bright lighting on the part
content.explanation: Handling or contact can locally rearrange the field on a magnetized part, producing fuzzy particle patterns unrelated to any flaw. Demagnetizing and reprocessing can clear it.
distractors: A true crack is a relevant indication, not magnetic writing.
Proper demagnetization removes, not causes, magnetic writing.
Lighting is unrelated to magnetic writing.

content.stem: Strong particle buildup at the ends of a longitudinally magnetized part is usually:
options: A nonrelevant effect from the end poles
A real crack right at the end of the part
Always a clearly rejectable flaw
Caused by the bright white light
content.explanation: Longitudinal magnetization creates poles at the part ends that attract particles. This end-pole buildup is nonrelevant, not a flaw.
distractors: End-pole buildup is a field effect, not a crack.
It is nonrelevant, not a rejectable flaw.
White light does not cause particle buildup.

content.stem: An indication that follows a hardness or heat-affected boundary may be due to:
options: A change in magnetic permeability, not a flaw
Always a real crack running along the boundary
An error in the lighting setup used
A part that had been demagnetized
content.explanation: Abrupt permeability changes (for example at a weld heat-affected zone or hardness boundary) can produce indications that are not flaws, which must be recognized and evaluated.
distractors: Such boundary indications are not always cracks.
It is a magnetic effect, not a lighting error.
A demagnetized part would not hold this indication; it is a field effect.

content.stem: To help confirm whether an indication is real, a technician may:
options: Clean, demagnetize, and reinspect to see if it returns
Simply ignore the indication and move right on
Paint over the indication entirely
Greatly increase the ambient room light level by a lot
content.explanation: Reprocessing can show whether an indication is a true flaw (it reappears) or a false one such as magnetic writing (it clears). Evaluation remains a higher-level step.
distractors: Ignoring the indication does not resolve it.
Painting over hides the surface and is not done.
Greatly increasing ambient light defeats fluorescent viewing.

content.stem: On finding an indication, the Level I technician generally:
options: Recognizes and records it for higher-level evaluation
Dispositions it himself as either accept or reject right away
Writes the formal acceptance criteria for it himself
Approves the part for return to service
content.explanation: A Level I recognizes and records indications; evaluating them against acceptance criteria and dispositioning the part are Level II or III responsibilities.
distractors: Disposition (accept/reject) is above the Level I scope.
Acceptance criteria come from codes and higher levels.
Approving the part is not a Level I function.

content.stem: Indications should be viewed:
options: Close enough and with enough light to see them clearly
From clear across the whole room, entirely much too far
Through tinted dark glass under bright white light
Without ever looking at the surface
content.explanation: The technician views the surface closely under the proper light so indications are clearly seen and not missed.
distractors: Across the room is too far to see fine indications.
Tinted glass in white light is not the correct viewing setup.
The surface must be observed to find indications.

content.stem: To avoid missing indications, the technician should:
options: View the whole required area, overlapping as needed
Spot-check just one small single area of the whole part
Look only along the outer edges
Rely on memory of other similar parts
content.explanation: Complete viewing of the inspection area, with overlap, ensures indications anywhere in the area are seen.
distractors: Spot-checking can miss flaws elsewhere.
Edges alone are not full coverage.
Each part is viewed; memory of other parts is not a substitute.

content.stem: MT personnel typically must meet a near-vision requirement such as:
options: Reading a specified small type size, such as a Jaeger chart
Being fully color blind in order to view the parts properly
Meeting no near-vision requirement of any kind whatsoever
Having only good long-distance vision and nothing else
content.explanation: A near-vision check (often a Jaeger near-vision standard) confirms the technician can resolve small indications. The exact requirement comes from the governing specification.
distractors: Color blindness is a limitation, not a requirement.
Vision requirements do apply to NDT personnel.
Near vision, not only distance vision, is the relevant requirement.

content.stem: For visible (color-contrast) MT, color vision matters because:
options: The technician must tell the particle color from the surface
Color is never actually used in any magnetic particle testing
Only fluorescent inspection work ever makes use of color
Color vision does not matter at all for any of this work
content.explanation: Visible inspection relies on seeing the particle color against the surface, so adequate color perception supports reliable detection. Specifications set the requirement.
distractors: Color contrast is central to visible inspection.
Visible work also depends on color perception, not only fluorescent.
Color vision is relevant to color-contrast inspection.

content.stem: Vision requirements for NDT personnel are typically:
options: Checked periodically per the written practice
Checked just one single time in a whole lifetime
Never checked at any point at all
Set only by the part supplier
content.explanation: Vision is verified on a defined interval under the employer's written practice so personnel continue to meet the requirement.
distractors: A single lifetime check does not ensure ongoing acuity.
Vision is checked, not ignored.
The written practice, not the part supplier, sets vision requirements.

content.stem: Indications may be recorded by:
options: Written notes, sketches, photos, or transfer methods
From memory alone, with no written record kept at all
By erasing all the indications first
By demagnetizing the whole part first
content.explanation: Common recording methods include written notes, sketches, photographs, and tape or lacquer transfers, capturing the indication before cleaning removes it.
distractors: Memory alone is not a reliable record.
Erasing the indication destroys what is to be recorded.
Demagnetizing first can disturb the indication before recording.

content.stem: A useful indication record includes:
options: Location, length or size, orientation, and number
Only the date of the whole inspection, nothing else
The inspector's lunch break that day
Nothing specific about it at all
content.explanation: Recording location, size, orientation, and quantity supports later evaluation and traceability of what was found.
distractors: The date alone omits the indication details.
Irrelevant personal notes are not part of the record.
Specific indication details are the point of the record.

content.stem: Before applying particles, the technician confirms the surface temperature is:
options: Within the limits for the particle materials used
Always somewhere well above the boiling point of water
Irrelevant to the whole inspection
Always well below the freezing point
content.explanation: Particle materials have temperature limits; wet baths can flash off on hot parts, so the surface must be within the qualified range, or dry powder rated for the temperature is used.
distractors: Above boiling would damage wet baths and many materials.
Temperature does affect particle behavior and safety.
Below freezing is not a general requirement and can cause other issues.

content.stem: The surface must be clean enough that:
options: Indications are visible and particles move freely
It merely looks shiny and clean enough to the eye
It is fully covered over in paint
It is coated in a thin film of oil
content.explanation: Cleanliness ensures particles reach flaws and indications can be seen; heavy soil, paint, or oil interferes.
distractors: Appearance alone is not the goal; particle mobility and visibility are.
Paint can mask indications.
Oil interferes with particle mobility and visibility.

content.stem: When removing excess dry powder, the technician must avoid:
options: Blowing so hard that real indications come off
Using only a gentle and steady stream of air
Leaving the particles held at the flaws
Observing the part properly while under the field
content.explanation: A gentle air stream clears loose excess while leaving indications intact. Too forceful removal can strip genuine indications.
distractors: A gentle air stream is the correct technique.
Particles held at flaws should remain; that is the indication.
Observing under the field is correct practice.

content.stem: Excessive background during inspection should be:
options: Reduced, by correct concentration and field, so flaws stand out
Increased even further across the whole part surface area
Simply ignored entirely during the whole inspection process
Recorded as if it were a real rejectable flaw indication
content.explanation: High background masks indications, so concentration, field strength, and cleanliness are controlled to keep it low. Background is not itself a flaw.
distractors: Increasing background further hides indications.
Ignoring heavy background risks missing flaws.
Background is not a discontinuity.

content.stem: In fluorescent inspection, gloves, oils, or marker inks that fluoresce can:
options: Cause confusing background and false indications
Improve the overall inspection sensitivity a lot
Magnetize the part that is being tested
Take the place of the UV viewing lamp
content.explanation: Stray fluorescing materials add background and false signals, so cleanliness and suitable consumables are maintained for fluorescent work.
distractors: Extraneous fluorescence hurts, not helps, sensitivity.
Fluorescing contaminants do not magnetize the part.
They do not replace the UV lamp.

content.stem: A surface crack indication typically appears as:
options: A sharp, well-defined line of built-up particles
A broad, fuzzy smear of loose scattered particles
No particle buildup on it at all
A change in the part's surface color
content.explanation: Surface-breaking cracks produce sharp, tightly defined particle lines. Broader, fuzzier patterns more often suggest subsurface conditions.
distractors: A broad fuzzy pattern more often indicates a subsurface condition.
A crack produces particle buildup, not none.
The indication is a particle pattern, not a color change in the metal.

content.stem: Compared with a surface crack, a slightly subsurface flaw usually gives an indication that is:
options: Broader and less sharply defined
Sharper and more tightly defined
Completely invisible every time
Brightly colored on the part
content.explanation: Leakage from a subsurface flaw spreads before reaching the surface, so its indication is broader and fuzzier than a sharp surface-crack line.
distractors: Sharper, tighter indications are typical of surface cracks.
Subsurface flaws within range can still be seen.
Indication appearance is about pattern, not bright color.

content.stem: After recognizing and recording indications, the next responsibility is:
options: Evaluation against acceptance criteria by qualified staff
Immediate scrapping done by the Level I technician on his own
Painting over the part right away
Shipping it out without any review
content.explanation: Recorded indications are evaluated against the acceptance standard by Level II or III personnel to decide disposition.
distractors: Scrapping is a disposition decision above the Level I scope.
Painting is not part of evaluation.
Shipping without evaluation skips a required step.

content.stem: Interpreting an indication means deciding:
options: Whether it is relevant, nonrelevant, or false
Whether the whole part is to be accepted or not
The acceptance limits set for the part
The magnetizing current value to use
content.explanation: Interpretation sorts indications into relevant, nonrelevant, or false. Evaluating relevant indications against criteria (acceptance) is a separate, higher-level step.
distractors: Deciding acceptance is evaluation, not interpretation, and is above the Level I.
Acceptance limits come from the specification.
Magnetizing current is a setup parameter, not an interpretation.

content.stem: Which statement about MT inspection is correct?
options: Use proper light, sort relevant, nonrelevant, false, then record
Any indication found is automatically a rejectable flaw, every time
The lighting level does not matter at all here
The Level I technician sets the acceptance criteria
content.explanation: Adequate lighting (white light or UV-A), correct recognition of indication types, and proper recording support evaluation. Not every indication is a flaw, and criteria are set above the Level I.
distractors: Nonrelevant and false indications are not rejectable flaws.
Lighting level is essential to seeing indications.
Acceptance criteria are not set by the Level I.

content.stem: Demagnetization is performed when residual magnetism could:
options: Interfere with later machining, welding, or measurement
Actually improve the later inspection process itself somehow
Make the whole part weigh less
Change the painted surface color of the part
content.explanation: A leftover field can attract chips, deflect instruments, cause weld arc blow, or hold debris in service, so it is removed when it would cause problems.
distractors: Residual field after inspection does not improve later work.
Demagnetization does not change the part's weight.
It does not change the part color.

content.stem: Residual magnetism can cause arc blow, which is a problem during:
options: Welding the part
Painting the part
Weighing the part
Visual inspection
content.explanation: A residual field can deflect the welding arc (arc blow), so magnetized parts are demagnetized before welding.
distractors: Painting is not affected by arc blow.
Weighing is not affected by arc blow.
Visual inspection is not affected by arc blow.

content.stem: Residual magnetism during machining can cause:
options: Chips and filings clinging to the part and tooling
Noticeably faster cutting of the steel part
A noticeably better surface finish
No real effect on the machining process at all anyway
content.explanation: A magnetized part holds chips and filings, fouling the work and tooling, which is one reason to demagnetize before machining.
distractors: Clinging chips do not speed cutting.
Clinging debris worsens, not improves, finish.
Residual magnetism does affect machining.

content.stem: Demagnetization may be unnecessary when:
options: The part will be remagnetized or the residual field is harmless
Always, in absolutely every single case without any exception
Never, since demagnetization is always strictly required anyway
The part simply happens to be made of ferromagnetic steel
content.explanation: If the part will be remagnetized or heated past its Curie point, or the residual field will not affect service, demagnetization may not be needed. The procedure defines the requirement.
distractors: Demagnetization is not always skippable; it depends on the situation.
It is not always required; it depends on downstream effects.
Being ferromagnetic does not by itself decide the need to demagnetize.

content.stem: A common demagnetization method is to:
options: Pass the part through an AC coil and slowly withdraw it
Apply one single steady and very strong constant DC field
Heat it up slightly during the whole test
Spray it down with the particle bath
content.explanation: Passing the part through an AC coil and slowly withdrawing it lets the part experience a diminishing alternating field, reducing the residual field toward zero.
distractors: A steady strong DC field magnetizes rather than demagnetizes.
Slight heating does not reliably demagnetize below the Curie point.
Spraying bath does not demagnetize the part.

content.stem: When demagnetizing with an AC coil, the part is withdrawn slowly so that:
options: The field it sees decreases gradually to a low value
The whole magnetizing field simply stops dead all at once
The part heats up a lot during it
The part gains an even stronger field
content.explanation: Gradually moving the part away from the coil exposes it to a steadily weakening alternating field, which leaves little residual magnetism.
distractors: A sudden stop can leave a residual field.
Demagnetization is not about heating.
Done correctly it weakens, not strengthens, the field.

content.stem: Parts magnetized with DC are often demagnetized using:
options: Reversing and gradually decreasing DC
A single one-shot DC current pulse
Bright white light shone on the part
A pie gauge held on the surface
content.explanation: Reversing the DC direction while stepping the current down drives the residual field toward zero, reaching deeper than AC demagnetization.
distractors: A single DC pulse magnetizes rather than demagnetizes.
Light does not demagnetize the part.
A pie gauge indicates field; it does not demagnetize.

content.stem: AC demagnetization is effective mainly for surface residual fields, while deeper residual fields may require:
options: DC step-down, reversing and decreasing the field
No corrective action of any kind taken at all
Still more AC current applied every single time
Bright white light shone on the part
content.explanation: Because AC concentrates at the surface, deep residual fields from DC magnetization are better removed by reversing, decreasing DC.
distractors: Deep residual fields are not removed by doing nothing.
AC may not reach deep residual fields regardless of amount.
Light does not demagnetize.

content.stem: After demagnetizing, the residual field should be:
options: Checked with a field indicator or gauss meter
Simply assumed to be exactly zero gauss already
Measured using a white light meter
Ignored entirely after demagnetizing
content.explanation: A gauss meter or field indicator verifies the residual field is below the allowed limit, confirming demagnetization was effective.
distractors: The field is verified, not assumed.
A light meter measures light, not magnetic field.
Residual field is checked, not ignored, when demagnetization is required.

content.stem: The acceptable residual field level is:
options: Specified by the procedure or specification
Any value at all is considered perfectly fine
Set by the magnetic particle color
Unlimited, with no upper bound at all
content.explanation: Specifications set a maximum residual field; the technician verifies the part is below it where demagnetization is required.
distractors: Any value is not acceptable; a limit applies.
Particle color does not set the residual-field limit.
Residual field is limited, not unlimited, when control is required.

content.stem: A periodic system performance check can be done with a:
options: A Ketos (Betz) test ring
A long steel measuring tape
A simple glass thermometer
A small handheld stopwatch
content.explanation: The Ketos ring, with known subsurface holes, checks that particles and equipment together produce the expected indications, verifying system performance.
distractors: A tape measure checks dimensions, not system performance.
A thermometer measures temperature.
A stopwatch measures time.

content.stem: Field direction and adequacy in an area are commonly verified with:
options: A QQI shim or a pie gauge
A radiographic film densitometer
A precision dial micrometer
A calibrated torque wrench
content.explanation: QQIs/shims and pie gauges confirm an adequate field of the correct direction at the surface during setup and checks.
distractors: A densitometer reads radiographic film density.
A micrometer measures dimensions.
A torque wrench measures fastener torque.

content.stem: A routine check that a yoke is working is the:
options: A lift test with a set weight at maximum pole spacing
A simple color test carried out on the magnetic yoke device
A simple sound test of the yoke
A simple smell test of the yoke
content.explanation: Lifting a specified test weight at maximum leg spacing confirms the yoke develops adequate magnetizing force. Confirm the weight against the specification.
distractors: There is no color test for yoke function.
There is no standard sound test for yoke lift.
There is no smell test for yoke function.

content.stem: Wet bath concentration is checked routinely using a:
options: A settling (centrifuge) tube
A handheld magnetic gauss meter
A handheld UV-A radiometer
A handheld magnetic yoke
content.explanation: The settling tube reading verifies the bath particle concentration stays within the procedure range as a routine check.
distractors: A gauss meter reads field, not concentration.
A UV radiometer reads UV-A, not concentration.
A yoke magnetizes; it does not check concentration.

content.stem: UV-A and white-light levels are:
options: Verified periodically with calibrated meters
Checked just one single time and then never again
Estimated by the naked eye alone
Not really part of MT at all
content.explanation: Light levels are verified on a schedule with calibrated meters so viewing conditions remain adequate for valid inspection.
distractors: A single check does not catch later lamp degradation.
Eye estimation is not a valid verification.
Lighting verification is part of MT.

content.stem: A key electrical safety practice in MT is:
options: Proper grounding and cable care, especially when wet
Working barefoot while standing in deep pooled water
Ignoring any frayed or damaged cables
Bypassing all of the safety interlocks
content.explanation: MT uses electrical equipment, so grounding, cable care, and caution in wet conditions reduce shock hazards. Damaged cables and bypassed interlocks are unsafe.
distractors: Working barefoot in water raises shock risk.
Frayed cables are a shock hazard and must be addressed.
Bypassing interlocks defeats built-in protections.

content.stem: To reduce prod arc and burn hazards, the technician should:
options: Keep good contact and follow limits on where prods go
Use poor, loose contact at the tips
Apply prods on any critical finished part surface at all
Increase the current without any limit
content.explanation: Good contact reduces arcing, and many specifications restrict prods on critical or finished surfaces because arc strikes can damage them.
distractors: Poor contact increases arcing and burns.
Critical finished surfaces are often off-limits for prods.
Unlimited current increases overheating and burn risk.

content.stem: When using oil-based wet baths, the technician should consider:
options: Flash point, ventilation, and ignition sources
Nothing in particular to even consider at all
That the oil carrier is always fully nonflammable
Using it right near an open flame
content.explanation: Petroleum-distillate carriers can be flammable, so flash point, ventilation, and keeping ignition sources away are important.
distractors: Flammable carriers require specific precautions.
Many oil carriers are flammable.
Using flammable carriers near open flame is hazardous.

content.stem: UV-A exposure precautions include:
options: Not staring into the beam and protecting eyes and skin
Deliberately looking straight into the bright UV lamp directly
Removing all of the eye protection
Aiming the beam right at the face
content.explanation: UV-A can affect eyes and skin, so the beam is not viewed directly and appropriate protection is used.
distractors: Looking into the lamp is hazardous.
Protection should be used, not removed.
Aiming UV-A at the face is unsafe.

content.stem: Good practice with MT chemicals and carriers includes:
options: Adequate ventilation and following the safety data sheets
Completely ignoring all of the safety data sheets entirely
Mixing the chemicals together at random
Working with no ventilation at all
content.explanation: Following safety data sheets and ensuring ventilation protects against vapor and contact hazards from carriers and conditioners.
distractors: Safety data sheets give required handling information and are followed.
Random mixing of chemicals is unsafe.
Ventilation is important when using carriers and solvents.

content.stem: Used particles, baths, and rags should be:
options: Handled and disposed of per applicable requirements
Poured straight down any nearby open floor drain outside
Left lying around on the floor
Burned indoors right after use
content.explanation: Spent materials are managed and disposed of according to environmental and safety rules, not dumped or handled carelessly.
distractors: Pouring baths down a drain may violate disposal rules.
Leaving materials on the floor is a slip and contamination hazard.
Burning materials indoors is unsafe.

content.stem: MT records typically capture:
options: The part, procedure, parameters, indications, and personnel
Only the outdoor weather conditions on that particular day
Nothing of any kind at all about the actual inspection job
The inspector's own personal car and travel details
content.explanation: Documentation ties the inspection to the part, the procedure and parameters used, what was found, and who performed it, supporting traceability.
distractors: Weather is not the content of an MT record.
Records are required, not empty.
Irrelevant personal details are not the record content.

content.stem: In the overall process, demagnetization is performed:
options: After inspection and recording, when required
Before ever cleaning the whole part at all first
Before magnetizing the whole part
In place of recording the results
content.explanation: The part is inspected and indications recorded first, then demagnetized when a residual field would cause downstream problems.
distractors: Cleaning precedes magnetizing; demagnetizing follows inspection.
Demagnetizing before magnetizing is out of sequence.
Demagnetization does not replace recording.

content.stem: If a residual-field check fails the limit after demagnetization, the technician should:
options: Repeat or adjust the demagnetization and recheck
Ship the part straight out the door anyway, regardless
Ignore the failing reading completely
Increase the magnetizing current more
content.explanation: A failed residual-field check means the part is still too magnetized, so demagnetization is repeated or adjusted and the field rechecked against the limit.
distractors: Shipping a part that fails the residual limit is improper.
The reading must be addressed, not ignored.
Adding magnetizing current increases, not reduces, the residual field.

content.stem: Routine system performance checks (test ring, QQI, yoke lift, settling tube, light meters) exist to:
options: Confirm the equipment and materials still perform well
Decorate the inspection laboratory
Take the place of the whole written inspection procedure
Set the formal acceptance criteria
content.explanation: Periodic checks catch degraded lamps, weak yokes, off baths, or poor field before they cause missed flaws, keeping the system valid.
distractors: Checks have a functional purpose, not decoration.
Checks support, not replace, the procedure.
Checks verify performance; they do not set acceptance criteria.

content.stem: Magnetizing cables and contacts should be:
options: Inspected for damage and kept in good condition
Used right up until they completely fail and break
Frayed on purpose to make them flexible
Wrapped tightly around the inspector
content.explanation: Damaged cables and poor contacts create electrical and arcing hazards and unreliable current, so they are inspected and maintained.
distractors: Using cables until failure invites hazards and downtime.
Fraying is damage, not a feature.
Wrapping live cables around a person is unsafe.

content.stem: Appropriate personal protection in MT may include:
options: UV-blocking eyewear, gloves, and protection for the chemicals
No protective equipment of any single kind whatsoever at all
Only a single hard hat worn in every single case
Open sandals worn while standing right near the chemical baths
content.explanation: PPE is selected for the hazards present, such as UV eyewear for fluorescent work and gloves for carriers, in addition to general site requirements.
distractors: Some protection is appropriate given the hazards.
A hard hat alone may not address UV or chemical hazards.
Open footwear near baths is a contact and slip hazard.

content.stem: Heating a ferromagnetic part above its Curie point will:
options: Remove its magnetism until the part cools again
Permanently strengthen its magnetic field instead
Have no real effect on the part
Make the part become radioactive
content.explanation: Above the Curie temperature a material loses its ferromagnetism; this is why parts heat-treated above that point need no separate demagnetization for that step. This is background knowledge, not a routine demagnetizing method.
distractors: Heating above the Curie point removes, not strengthens, the field.
It has a clear effect: loss of ferromagnetism.
Heating does not make the part radioactive.

content.stem: Regarding safety and checks, the Level I technician:
options: Follows safety rules and runs routine checks under direction
Writes out the entire facility safety program himself, alone
Approves all of the waste disposal permits himself
Sets all the calibration intervals
content.explanation: A Level I follows established safety practices and performs routine equipment and material checks, recording them, while program-level decisions rest with higher levels and other functions.
distractors: Writing the safety program is not a Level I function.
Approving disposal permits is outside the Level I role.
Setting calibration intervals is above the Level I.

content.stem: Which statement is correct?
options: Demagnetize when needed, verify it, keep equipment checked, work safely
Never demagnetize the finished part at all, under any circumstances
Just skip all of the routine equipment checks to save some time
Completely ignore both the electrical and the UV light hazards
content.explanation: Parts are demagnetized when a residual field would interfere downstream, the result is verified, equipment and materials are checked routinely, and electrical, chemical, and UV hazards are controlled.
